title: Federal Court rules Lorella Springs Wilderness Park tourism permit invalid
text:
Northern Territory native title holders are claiming a "hard fought win" after a Federal Court judge ruled a tourism permit for Lorella Springs Wilderness Park is invalid, and ordered the Pastoral Land Board to reassess the application.

For about two decades, the owners of Lorella Springs, a 400,000-hectare outback cattle station located about 1,000 kilometres from Darwin, ran a significant tourism business with accommodation, a bar, fishing, swimming and helicopter tours.

The station, about 2.5 times the size of London, is also home to protected sacred, burial and ceremony sites.

But the station has been closed to most tourists since January 2023. Only a select number of guided tours have been allowed to visit, with the owners citing "bureaucracy" becoming "too much" to sustain operations.

Lorella Springs Wilderness Park was a tourist hotspot before it was closed to most visitors in 2023. (Supplied: Carmen Brown)

In 2022, owners Marie and Rhett Walker lodged an application for a "farm tourism operations" permit. Their application said Aboriginal sites would "be avoided from all tourism activity".

The owners also applied to extract water from Rosie Creek.

The Pastoral Land Board granted the permit and the water licence — but in 2025, the Northern Land Council (NLC), on behalf of Burdal Riley, Murrungun Wunubari and Mambali Walangara native title holders, challenged the NT government's decision to grant those.

Concerned that sacred sites in the area had been interfered with in the past, the native title holders argued the tourism activities involved the "observation of Aboriginal cultural works and activities".

They also argued the government had been "unreasonable and irrational" in its decision-making process and failed to consider the presence of threatened species and other environmental issues.

In handing down her lengthy judgement on Friday, Justice Natalie Charlesworth considered the native title holders' 12 arguments.

The wilderness park spans hundreds of thousands of hectares. (Supplied: Lorella Springs Wilderness Park)

She found that when the Pastoral Land Board ultimately approved a permit covering about 60,000 hectares — an area far larger than what was applied for — it "exceeded its jurisdiction".

"The circumstances in which that came about are not at all clear," she said.

She also found there had been no comprehensive environmental impact assessment done of the entire area and that the board "failed to comply with its obligation to afford procedural fairness" to native title holders.

Justice Charlesworth declared the permit invalid largely on those points, and ordered the board to reassess the application "according to law", which means a new permit could be issued in future.

Some arguments rejected

The native title holders also argued the permit did not qualify as "farm tourism" under section 24GB of the Native Title Act, as there was "no substantive connection to pastoral activities".

Justice Charlesworth said she was informed the matter was the first time a court had been forced to consider the section — which allows certain activities like farm tourism or running cattle to go ahead on pastoral land without agreement from native title holders, but rules out other types of tourism involving observing Aboriginal activities or cultural works.

Tourism permit under review for NT's Lorella Springs Wilderness Park The future of an isolated tourism hotspot home to stunning waterfalls and ancient rock art is uncertain following a Federal Court hearing in Darwin.

She noted there was "public interest in the resolution of the issue given the likelihood that it may arise again", with large swathes of the NT and South Australia covered by pastoral leases.

However, Justice Charlesworth rejected the argument, finding the activities on offer at Lorella Springs "all fall within the phrase 'farm tourism activities'."

The native title holders also argued the permit was invalid because it permitted "tourism activities that involved observing the activities or cultural works of Aboriginal people".

Justice Charlesworth "unreservedly" accepted evidence about the "hurt and distress" felt by native title holders over how tourism at Lorella Springs could impact sacred sites, but ultimately dismissed that argument as well.

"The focus of [section] 24GB is upon what has been authorised by the Board, not upon what may happen in the future by reason of feared unauthorised actions of the [owners] or tourists," she said.

Justice Charlesworth upheld the water licence, ruling she was not satisfied it would affect native title because there was no evidence the amount of water extracted would affect native title holders' ability to take water.

Matthew Ryan says the legal battle over Lorella Springs has been "hard fought". (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

NLC chair Matthew Ryan called the judgement a "hard fought win" for native title holders.

"Protecting sacred sites is protecting culture. It is always necessary to work with the caretakers of precious country to keep these sacred areas safe," he said.

A spokesperson for the NT government did not respond to questions about whether Lorella Springs would re-open in the future but said it "will take the time to carefully consider the Federal Court's decision."

title: Australia bowls first as rising star Beardman is rested following stunning debut
text:
Australian paceman Mahli Beardman, two days after his stunning one-day international debut, has been rested for the second clash against England.

Beardman claimed 6-24 to lead Australia to a seven-wicket victory against England in the series opener in Perth on Friday.

But the 21-year-old, whose figures were the fourth best by a debutant in ODI history, has been managed for Sunday's Adelaide Oval fixture, with Riley Meredith summoned as his replacement.

Australia won the toss and opted to field, with Tasmanian quick Meredith a fresh addition to the squad for the ODI series, which concludes on Wednesday in Hobart.

"It's no secret we like to chase. We know the wicket stays really good here in Adelaide," captain Mitch Marsh said after the toss.

"Hopefully we can get the most out it of early and then chase it down under lights.

"Mahli Beardman, young kid, tough to back up on 48 hours turnaround. He rests today."

Meredith's replacement of Beardman was the sole change to the Australian team that downed the Poms in Perth.

England also made a change, with Jamie Overton out and 23-year-old paceman Sonny Bell included.

After the ODI series, the Australians play five T20 games against England from next Saturday, with paceman Nathan Ellis out of that series as he continues to recover from a side strain suffered on the recent tour of South Africa.

NSW left-armer Ben Dwarshuis has been called into the T20 squad.

AAP

title: Aussie quick says 'everyone knew' about sandpaper, as Warner doubles down
text:
Former Australian cricketer Chadd Sayers, who played his lone Test after Sandpapergate on the infamous 2018 South African tour, has said he is comfortable stating he believed everyone in the team knew about ball-tampering.

The notorious Cape Town Test match, where Cameron Bancroft was filmed using sandpaper on the cricket ball, was thrust into the spotlight this week after Usman Khawaja in his memoir, Sabr, claimed ball-tampering was commonplace and the entire team needed to take responsibility.

The memoir has caused a rift in Australian cricket.

David Warner, who was suspended with Cameron Bancroft and then-captain Steve Smith over the incident, backed Khawaja's account in Sabr, saying it was "100 per cent accurate".

Meanwhile, Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Sayers, who was part of the Australian touring squad in 2018, said ahead of Australia's second ODI against England in Adelaide on Sunday that he was comfortable saying every member of the team knew sandpaper was being used.

"I'm comfortable saying where I'm sitting now that everyone knew what was going on [in South Africa in 2018]," Sayers said on the SEN broadcast.

"It [sandpaper] was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in change rooms … I'm not taking sides; it's just my recollection of what took place."

Sayers also said there was a meeting held in the wake of the team being caught with sandpaper, which lasted between 60 and 90 minutes.

Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Test match in Cape Town, with an investigation determining he, Smith and vice-captain Warner were responsible for the ball tampering.

The trio was suspended, while the bowlers in that Test have always denied knowledge that sandpaper was being used on the ball.

In his memoir, Khawaja claimed he knew sandpaper was being used on the ball and told Bancroft to be careful.

Khawaja also said ball-tampering was commonplace in cricket.

Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

"When he says 'we all knew', if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins said on Friday.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years; I did not know that was happening.

"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper; that's complete and utter nonsense.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book Ussie's been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell a story, 100 per cent. I'm really glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Warner doubles down on Cricket Australia on social media

David Warner has hit out at Cricket Australia as Sandpapergate continues to dominate headlines. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

David Warner has made another statement on social media, claiming he was not aware of all the facts before taking the brunt of punishment for Sandpapergate.

On Saturday, Warner accused Cricket Australia of a potential cover-up by claiming he believed the bowlers were not interviewed by the organisation about the incident.

Cape Town inquiry spoke to all Aussie bowlers, ABC understands Sources connected to the Australian bowling group say they all spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into Cape Town ball tampering, which runs counter to claims by David Warner.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," he wrote on Instagram.

"If that's correct then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning … ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Multiple media outlets, including ABC Sport, have reported the bowlers were interviewed by Cricket Australia.

On Sunday, Warner then doubled down on his criticism of Cricket Australia and supported his previous post.

Loading Instagram content

"Just to clarify 'As far as I am aware' was the POINT," he wrote.

"I was never told the bowlers had been interviewed or provided statements.

"That information would've been pretty useful when I was forced to make decisions back in 2018.

"Why weren't we given all the evidence by CA?"

title: Australian doctors say health anxiety is being fuelled by social media
text:
Ashley Bowden spends a large part of his workday counselling patients for their health anxiety in his regional NSW practice.

"It almost feels as if it's 50 per cent of the patients I see; we end up touching on health anxiety," he said.

"There's certainly a number of patients that have quite severe anxiety around their health."

Ashley Bowden is a GP in regional NSW. (Supplied: Ashley Bowden)

Dr Bowden said social media was fuelling the issue.

"I absolutely love talking to patients about what they've seen online … what they're worrying about and what's causing them to spiral," he said.

Olivia Loughnan completed her PhD on the link between social media and health anxiety. (Supplied: Olivia Loughnan)

Psychologist Olivia Loughnan said social media played a "significant" role in triggering health anxiety.

She said algorithms reinforced health-related fears by responding to what users watched, searched for and engaged with.

"Someone who watches a video about the early warning signs of a serious illness, they may subsequently be exposed to more content about related symptoms," Dr Loughnan said.

"It can create the impression that serious illnesses are increasingly common or personally relevant to them."

Predictive tests advertised online

Dr Bowden said the online marketing of predictive medical tests and health screenings, such as full body MRI scans or blood tests, was also playing a role.

"I have a lot of patients that are on supplements or they're undertaking private tests at huge expense," he said.

" It can lead to a huge amount of health anxiety. "

The products are part of the world of longevity, biohacking and health optimisation, which has a strong following online.

There's anti-aging hype. Then there's the science showing real promise Biohacking and anti-aging science are raising hopes of living longer. What's hype and what shows promise?

Dr Loughnan said the trends could be positive by encouraging people to be more proactive about their health and wellbeing.

"However, the concern is that pursuit of that optimal health can become excessive," she said.

"When people are constantly exposed to information about hidden diseases, prevention scans, biological aging … they can begin to feel that being healthy is simply not enough."

She said it reinforced the idea that people should be constantly monitoring their bodies for symptoms.

"Psychologically, this can create heightened need for control, increased body monitoring and difficulty tolerating uncertainty," she said.

A woman at a biohacking conference in New York City. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

" There's a difference between taking reasonable steps to look after your health and becoming preoccupied with preventing every possible illness. "

Patients urged to talk to their GPs

Australian Medical Association president Michael Bonning said the tests were increasingly popular around the country.

"We see more patients seeking frequent or increasingly, not just comprehensive, but almost fringe investigations," Dr Bonning said.

"It's sometimes very difficult for a doctor to push back and say, 'No, you really shouldn't have that,' even though it is very clear that intervention or investigation doesn't have an evidence base to it."

Listen to the podcast It’s good to be on top of your health – but how far would you go to ensure you’re staying healthy?

An example of one of these tests being advertised online is full body MRI scans, which cost thousands of dollars and do not use radiation.

"It's really tempting to think that surely that's going to give us more information … we'll find the bad thing if it exists, whether it's a lump or a cancer," Dr Bowden said.

Dr Bonning and Dr Bowden said they were more likely to catch incidental findings, which could lead to false positives and invasive tests.

"There's no study that has demonstrated improved disease-specific survival from screening asymptomatic people without specific health risks," Dr Bonning said.

Dr Bowden said if people were concerned by something they had seen online, or were thinking about taking one of the tests, they should speak to a trusted GP.

"They can say, 'I've seen this online' or 'I've put it into an AI bot,' because that gives us a point of the conversation to talk around," he said.

He also said it was important to be critical of ads.

"Is the person marketing that in any way interested in improving their health, or do they have an ulterior motive like making money?" he said.

title: Tim Winton talks Rinehart, rage, climate change and Cloudstreet
text:
Tim Winton has been publishing books for more than 40 years, but there's one that stands out.

Cloudstreet — recently voted Australia's favourite book in an ABC poll — was a defining moment in Winton's career, but it's a book that almost never was.

"I get weird just thinking about it because it's those what-if, Sliding Doors kind of moments because I couldn't have rewritten it," he said.

In the late 1980s, Winton was in Europe with his wife and young son.

A young Tim Winton in 1998. (Supplied)

"We were in transit carrying all our earthly goods, and we were catching a bus to the airport in Rome, and we got off the bus," he said.

"We were just going into the terminal, and just before we got to the glass doors, this Italian guy started tugging on my sleeve … he's really quite insistent," Winton recalls.

"I stopped eventually, and he was pointing back at the bus and … there was one little grey sports bag in there, and I just couldn't believe it. It was all the manuscripts, all the type scripts, all the carbon copies, all the notes, my entire novel to that point about to head off into Rome unaccompanied.

"If it hadn't been for just the decency of that guy … I could have kissed him because, in a way, he saved our lives because that was the book that saved our lives."

The opening passage of Cloudstreet is set on the banks of Perth's Swan River, or Derbal Yerrigan. (ABC News: Courtney Bembridge)

Cloudstreet follows the fortunes of two families — the Lambs and the Pickles — over two decades in mid-20th-century Perth.

The book has been adapted for radio, theatre, opera and television, and in the 35 years since it was released, it has never been out of print.

"I can't really get my head around the life that the book has had," he said.

"I do have people coming up to me almost every day."

The opening passage from the book reads as follows:

"Will you look at us by the river! The whole restless mob of us on spread blankets in the dreamy briny sunshine skylarking and chiacking about for one day, one clear, clean, sweet day in a good world in the midst of our living." — Cloudstreet, 1992

Living in the era of rage

Winton told 7.30 people told him the book reminded them of a gentler time, a kinder country.

"Probably the most consistent thing that people say to me seems to be about the kind of decency that they see in it, a kind of a yearning for solidarity and neighbourliness," Winton said.

Tim Winton's Cloudstreet was voted Australia's favourite book in an ABC poll. (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

Winton's latest book, Songs from the Firefront, is a collection of personal essays exploring how people find meaning, community and hope in an era marked by climate change, rage and social upheaval.

"The book is me reflecting on my own anguish and my own rage," he said.

" The danger is that you just become so furious that you can't think and you can't hear anything … we can't converse with one another. We can't make any progress. "

He says the rise of big tech and the way algorithms seize on people's rage is feeding dangerous rhetoric, and those in charge need to be held accountable.

"People are profiting from our rage," Winton said.

"This is the thing that kills me. This is essentially a business model to make us angry, to make us scream at each other, to make us want to own each other, to destroy each other in public.

"I think the way our government at the moment is threatening to adopt a very supine attitude to those tech bros is a cause of deep concern … these bro-ligarchs or, as somebody very wisely has called it, the 'Nerd Reich'.

"I just think we need to be more assertive."

Big tech bosses are not the only ones who come in for criticism in his book.

He writes about his view of mining magnate Gina Rinehart in these words: "She does not value or understand: the natural world, tenderness, mercy, fellow feeling."

Tim Winton describes Gina Rinehart as a "lonely oligarch". (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Given Mrs Rinehart has a lot of power, Winton is asked if writing about her makes him nervous?

"I think everybody's nervous and careful in speaking about that person for those reasons, because there's just so much form," he said.

Winton went on to say it was hard to explain to people outside of Western Australia the influence that Mrs Rinehart, and her father Lang Hancock, had had "on every element of society in politics, in the media, in communications. The amount of fear and awe that they generate".

In June One Nation leader Pauline Hanson told the ABC that she consulted Mrs Rinehart on policy and considered her a friend.

And it was revealed in July that Mrs Rinehart paid for Senator Hanson's flights from London to Sicily earlier this year and arranged for her to attend high-end fashion shows.

Winton said he was concerned about Mrs Rinehart's growing political influence.

" It's the political ambition. It's the drive to force the country in a direction that clearly suits their interests. "

7.30 approached Mrs Rinehart for a response through her company. A spokesperson for Hancock Prospecting disagreed with Winton's views and suggested the author was promoting socialism.

"Tim needs to better understand, the socialist style causes he espouses, which are the very opposite of caring. And the very opposite of tenderness and mercy," the spokesperson told 7.30 in a statement.

"And Tim needs to understand, what does enable better outcomes: investment, innovation, and the opportunities these bring, lifting the standards of living of those fortunate enough not to live in his uncaring, merciless socialist utopias.

" If Tim actually gave a genuine damn about millions of Australians struggling and doing it tough, he'd be jumping on Mrs Rinehart's caring bandwagon. "

The spokesperson also stated that Mrs Rinehart and her companies had paid "$25 billion" in taxes over the past decade, which they said helped "provide for nurses, hospitals, police, veterans, the elderly, emergency services, defence and so much more for her fellow Australians".

"Sadly, Mrs Rinehart and Tim are likely to always disagree on the governments most important responsibility, defending our country and its citizens."

Loading...

A plea on climate change

Winton has been considering how the world should respond to rising temperatures for decades.

His 2024 novel, Juice, imagines a world where most of Australia is uninhabitable due to extreme weather.

"I know what it feels like at 50 degrees. I know what it feels like when the wind is blowing past 250 kilometres an hour in a category four cyclone, and you know what the smell of death is, the smell of a wildfire," he said.

"We had a generation to take swift and decisive climate action. We haven't done that.

Scorched land after bushfires that took place in Lancelin, Western Australia, 2023. ( ABC News: James Carmody )

"The best we can do now is to adapt and to mitigate the bits that we can. And sadly, we know that we're going to lose ecosystems, we're going to lose species, and a lot of people are going to live in more anguish and more straightened circumstances than needed to.

"And when you come from a prosperous country like ours, I don't think that's a tragedy. I think that's an outrage."

Tim Winton says the lack of action on climate change has been an "outrage". (ABC News: Courtney Bembridge)

As to why he wrote a memoir, a strange deviation for someone who is known to be very private, Winton said it was the right time.

"It's just a way of trying to sift through that stuff and figure things out and give an account of myself to myself as much as for anybody else," he said.

Tim Winton's mother with his young daughter. (Supplied)

"It's not really a proper memoir; it's just a sort of set of thoughts and reflections in the mode of memoir.

"You get to a sort of fulcrum point in your life where you realise there's more time behind you than years ahead of you, and that makes you reflect on where you've been … and what's most precious to you. And obviously that's the kids and their kids."

title: How Swim GP may have given a glimpse of the future of para-sport
text:
Swim GP's made for TV, all-action racing format has proven a hit with swimmers and spectators alike.

But the biggest benefit may well be the innovations that placed para-swimmers front and centre of the competition at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre.

In front of a sold-out crowd, four teams: Kraken, Wahoo, King Tide and Tsunami, competed in a variety of races ranging from skins events through to mystery medley relays.

Times are not important. It's all about who touches the wall first.

"It is an opportunity for our athletes, our Paralympic team and our Olympic team, to come together and really showcase what they do," Swimming Australia Paralympic head coach Mel Tantrum said ahead of Saturday's evening events.

"This is about building the brand, building the profile of the athletes, swimming in prime time in preparation for the next six years."

The Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre was sold-out for day two. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP is not a new idea, and indeed has built on the concepts reintroduced at last year's Australia vs the World in Brisbane.

However, crucially, Swim GP has seen para-swimmers take a leading role.

Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse told ABC Sport that involving the para-swimmers "was one of the most important factors" and a "no-brainer" in Swim GP's planning for a couple of reasons.

"Both our head coaches, Mel Tantrum and Rohan Taylor, they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials, ideally Sydney next year, but particularly the Olympic/Paralympic trials in '28 in Chandler, one of the reasons being, for the Olympics, SoFi Stadium, with 40,000 screaming Americans and Long Beach for the Paralympics," Woodhouse said.

"Some of those [para-]athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright lights, the flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"So there's quite an important benefit from Swim GP for those para-athletes that do have to deal with those things to get more accustomed to a noisy venue, to a bright flashy venue and things like that.

"[Also] that aspirational view that these athletes can provide, whether they're para-athletes or able-bodied athletes, to the young kids at home, and there's a lot of kids with various disabilities that don't have opportunities to get into a pool or to even just get involved in the other sports. So, just being able to showcase our amazing para-athletes and what they do is a really critical factor."

A big atmosphere is vital for Australia's swimmers to prepare for LA Olympic Games in 2028. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Tantrum agreed, saying integrating the two programs was vital.

"Swimming Australia is really inclusive in terms of the parity between Olympic and Paralympic programs and making sure our swimmers across both programs are really profiled and really supported," Tantrum said.

"The athletes are loving being part of a bigger team. Those sort of innovative, creative competitions make the athletes feel they're part of an elite team.

"It's not just para, it's not separate, it's part of being the Australian Dolphins swim team and both programs coming together.

"The athletes are fully integrated team members. They don't sit separately. They've got the same uniform, same bleachers, same team meetings.

"And I think that's, for the athletes, it's a chance for them to really showcase their athleticism.

"It's not about, oh, you're a para-athlete, it's about elite swimming at its best.

"The world's best swimmers are here in the pool. And yeah, whether you're Olympic or Paralympic, you know, able-bodied or have a disability, it doesn't matter. You're an elite athlete first and you're here to perform."

New tech bringing para-sport into the mainstream

Victoria Belando Nicholson (right) was a member of the King Tide team. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

One of the biggest challenges in para-sport when there are a limited number of athletes, is integrating multiple classifications and how to accurately, and fairly, ensure a level playing field.

In a standard multi-class meet, swimmers with varied impairments all start their races at the same time, with the winner determined by how close a swimmer gets to the world record in their particular classification.

That's all well and good but, for spectators, it can get confusing as to who as actually won because the winner does not always touch the wall first.

Swim GP gets around this by having a staggered start, with lights on the blocks for each swimmer.

The time-gap is determined based on a swimmer's season best in a particular distance and should result in a blanket finish — far more appealing for spectators.

"I think it's a really good idea to then see everyone come up towards each other and finish pretty closely," Paralympic legend Lakeisha Patterson told ABC Sport.

"It makes it an exciting race, I think, towards the end.

"I think for an event that isn't preparing for a world champs or a major international meet, this is really good for fans to see how multi-class swimming works."

Lakeisha Patterson said she was nervous before her race, perhaps made more so when Ben Hance literally ripped the shirt off his back when walking out. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson competed in, and won, Saturday night's opening race, a multi-class, mixed 100m event where each swimmer swam a different stroke, with Patterson unusually swimming butterfly, which she noted "definitely" won't be on her program for next year's world championships.

Perhaps she should reconsider. Patterson, who is classified as an S9 swimmer, swam a PB to blitz the field, although the other three swimmers; Tim Hodge (S9), Ben Hance (S14) and Keira Stephens (S10), were far closer together.

"It doesn't matter what their classification is and, in some cases, what their gender is," Tantrum explained.

"It's some new tech that we're trialling for the first time on the block so that athletes, no matter what their class or their gender, they can race together.

"With this [Swim GP] format, it's basically who touches the wall first is the winner.

"These staggered starts and close finals make the crowd get right into it. It makes it exciting if someone's got a 20-second stagger to catch up on in 100 metres. It makes for exciting racing, and the crowd really got into that last night and you could feel the crowd lift.

"That's what swimming should be, right? It should be exciting."

The future of para-sport?

Lakeisha Patterson (right) and Rowan Crothers (second right) were key members of Team Tsunami. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson noted that giving para-swimmers the same platform was crucial for the development of the sport.

"I think it's incredibly important to showcase that our athletes aren't just here for participation," she said.

"We are athletes showcasing what is possible, and I think Australia is leading the way in that inclusion space and how we can involve our entire team.

"Leading into Brisbane we can really build on that and hopefully have all of Australia behind us, and showing to the people watching at home that they may have a space in Paralympic sport as well."

Fully integrated competitions remain a rarity for para and able-bodied sporting events, the Commonwealth Games being a notable exception.

Given the success of this format, Tantrum said that innovations like the staggered starts seen in Swim GP could inspire more innovation elsewhere, perhaps even adding more athletes to future Commonwealth Games fields.

"If we could influence Commonwealth Games Federation … we could potentially have a greater number of athletes and a greater number of classes competing together," Tantrum said.

"We left a number of athletes at home [from the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games] because they simply didn't have events for those classes.

"So something that is more of a multi-class format for Commonwealth Games would be a great innovation to at least consider.

What should the future of para sport look like? Birmingham 2022 celebrated the largest para sport program in history, but there's still a large gap between wealthy and developing nations. What should integration look like?

"There's potential there that we could make this more integrated, fun, with exciting finishes and more athletes involved from Australia."

Perhaps even other sports could take note?

"Our immediate purpose is to showcase swimming," Tantrum said.

"But you know, if we can lead other sports and things like track and field to follow a similar format, where the para-athletes are standing alongside their Olympic athlete colleagues?

"You know, it's humans, right? It's human story, it's humans doing the best that they can do.

"If other sports such as athletics or cycling, want to come in and do what we're doing, if we're the trailblazers of that space, we'd love others to join in as well."

title: IVF, VAD and abortion off the table as Catholic company takes over hospital
text:
Accessing IVF, abortion or voluntary assisted dying (VAD) can be difficult and complicated. It can be harder still in rural and regional areas, where specialist shortages, long delays, distance and conscientious objection already limit access.

That is why a Catholic provider's decision to stop offering these services at Newcastle Private hospital in regional New South Wales has alarmed many clinicians and the community.

A local issue has exposed the potential for national implications. Calvary, a Catholic not-for-profit, is poised to take over 14 private hospitals from Healthscope, effectively doubling its private hospital network across the country.

Catholic providers already run about 6 per cent of Australia's public and private hospitals. If the latest Calvary deal clears regulators, that footprint will grow, and so will doctors' fears that access to legal healthcare will shrink.

These healthcare services have long attracted irreconcilable world views. But in 2026, they're legal. The debate now has moved beyond what should be lawful, to who decides what care should be available.

A regional takeover

The catalyst for the Calvary controversy was a Teams meeting held Wednesday before last. Obstetricians and gynaecologists at Newcastle Private met with their incoming Calvary leadership team.

Most were stunned when they were informed that IVF, abortion, VAD, gender affirming care, contraception, vasectomies and tubal ligation — to prevent fertility — would all be off the table within a few weeks.

Calvary is a Catholic not-for-profit health, aged-care and community-care organisation in Australia. It forms part of the ministry founded by the Sisters of the Little Company of Mary. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

The doctors had assumed they'd have time to negotiate terms or find a solution to keeping these services on the hospital site. No such luck.

They would also have to sign a document pledging to practise in line with the Code of Ethical Standards for Catholic Health and Aged Care Services in Australia. The code calls abortion "morally wrong" and says procedures that substitute for the "marital act" are "not morally permissible".

Calvary has acknowledged the "concerns and uncertainty within the community" and, late on Friday, more information was provided on its website.

"Where a requested intervention cannot be offered, we remain committed to treating every person with dignity, providing clear information and supporting access to appropriate ongoing care … Where a service is not offered, we will work with the treating specialist to support appropriate pathways."

The push to separate religion from healthcare

The Catholic church has been unwavering in its teachings for hundreds of years. Even as arguments on issues such as IVF and abortion have shifted, its stance has remained constant.

The code that guides decision-making in Catholic hospitals describes itself, in its preface, as "a crucial resource for the Church's mission in health care". In practice, that means the church expects that its core and fundamental beliefs on sanctity of life and medical intervention should be upheld in a hospital setting.

But critics say that approach can create more barriers to clinical care.

Calvary hospitals takeover nears Moments before surgery, Hayley Deniss was told about a potential disruption to her IVF care.

IVF Australia's Dr Veronica Knight calls Calvary's latest decision, "discrimination based on religious ethos".

The Royal Australia and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) is framing the issues as a matter of access, not ownership.

"We have no objection to Catholic ownership of hospitals," RANZCOG President Dr Nisha Khot told the ABC.

"What we're saying is that the law of the land says that all this health care is legal, and it should be available in every hospital. It should not be defined by the faith of the organisation that owns the hospital."

The competition regulator recently cleared Calvary's takeover of Hobart Private Hospital, where reproductive health, gender-affirming care and VAD were also due to be wound back.

RANZCOG'S concern is one of concentration. Dr Khot warned of scenarios "where the local public hospital and the private hospital are both Catholic", leaving no hospital access for reproductive sexual health care or voluntary assisted dying.

Postcode lottery

Newcastle already offers a preview of what happens when VAD care meets a Catholic operator.

The region's only public hospice sits within a hospital already run by Calvary as a public-private partnership. The hospital does not allow patients to have VAD drugs administered on-site, so patients who choose VAD must be moved to another bed — in another location — to die on their own terms.

Newcastle Private and Hunter Valley Private, the two hospitals Calvary is set to take over, have been making beds available where possible. If — or when — they stop offering that option, the pressure on health workers to find alternative beds will increase.

It's likely that Newcastle Private Hospital will no longer be able to take VAD patients, after being taken over by Calvary. (ABC Newcastle: Tamara Penniket)

One VAD doctor, who cannot be named because of their contract with NSW Health, says the result could be waits that "blow out by several days".

"There have already been cases where patients have been waiting for a couple of hours to transfer to another facility, in the final hours of their lives — sometimes in significant pain," the doctor said. "And the longer they must wait, the risk is that patient loses the capacity to consent to taking the medication."

Calvary's decision to end services at Newcastle Private and Hunter Valley Private would leave patients to rely on workarounds.

Clinicians typically go to great lengths to make those succeed, and most Newcastle patients will likely still get care, but with more administration, delay and frustration.

Dr Nisha Khot is concerned about the dangers of delays in healthcare for vulnerable people. (ABC News: Margaret Burin)

Delay comes with risks. RANZCOG's Dr Khot raises an extreme scenario, in which a woman at 18 weeks has her waters break at a Calvary hospital.

"She's 18 weeks at a Calvary hospital, isn't told about abortion as an option and doesn't realise her life is at risk until sepsis sets in," she said. This is hypothetical, but she says she's "genuinely concerned" about it happening.

Abortion access is already uneven, particularly in rural and regional NSW, where public hospitals have turned women away.

In public hospitals, governments have levers. After ABC reporting revealed that Orange Hospital had told staff to stop providing terminations of pregnancy, the NSW health minister stepped in and reinstated the service.

The answer is less clear when the hospital is private, whether it is Catholic or not.

Loading

No likely alternative

Calvary's supporters, and even those who reject its doctrine, argue the Catholic health sector is worth protecting. Its roots go back to nuns who began caring for the sick and dying in Sydney in the late 1800s.

Federal Labor MP and doctor Mike Freelander puts the practical question bluntly: "What's the alternative?"

In other words, if Calvary doesn't take over Healthscope's hospitals, who will, and who has the money to do it?

Dr Freelander says Catholic hospitals provide quality care, but is concerned the "Catholic ethical system is not keeping up with modern healthcare".

Labor MP and doctor Mike Freelander says we need Catholic providers to keep the hospitals going. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Some have called on NSW Health to refuse to transfer the hospital licence unless Calvary keeps providing the services it plans to end. The Health Minister and Premier have ruled that out, saying the services will be available elsewhere, including at an already stretched public hospital.

That has done little to reassure providers working to avoid scenarios like eggs for IVF being driven across town because women can no longer have them retrieved at the private hospital next door to the clinic where embryos are created.

The ACCC is still assessing Calvary's national expansion, but its test is whether the deal would substantially lessen competition, not whether patients lose access to services.

That leaves open the question: when care is legal, who decides whether or not it is provided?

title: Qld government reveals successful tenderer for $1.4b Brisbane Arena
text:
Construction of Brisbane's new entertainment and housing precinct is set to begin in January, with the state government selecting a private sector building partner.

Deputy premier Jarrod Bleijie announced this morning construction consortium Gather Brisbane had been chosen as the successful tenderer for the $1.4 billion Brisbane Arena in Woolloongabba.

The consortium includes Live Nation, Oak View Group, Plenary and Webuild, and beat out the Brisbane Entertainment Alliance consortium for the deal.

The Brisbane Arena is planned to have a 17,000-seat capacity, increasing to 18,700 for concerts.

The Brisbane Arena will be adjacent to the new Cross River Rail station and have capacity for up to 18,700 people. (Supplied)

The arena is intended to replace the Brisbane Entertainment Centre at Boondall in Brisbane's north and will be adjacent to the new Woolloongabba Cross River Rail station.

Mr Bleijie said the Gabba stadium nearby would be decommissioned following the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games, giving way to "open public space" and almost 4,000 new homes.

He said the government had committed a one-off $600 million contribution to the project's projected cost of $1.4 billion, to be delivered following its completion, which is expected in 2031.

"To get the acts to come to Queensland, to get the sporting events, to get the music events, the concerts to come to Queensland, you need a venue that rivals the rest of the venues around the world," he said.

"Entertainment lovers will love it, public transport users will be able to access the Cross River Rail here once it opens and I can say confidently … we look to be on-site in January."

Jarrod Bleijie says work on the new arena is expected to begin in January. (ABC News: Josh McIntosh)

He said the state would continue to own the land in a long-term commercial arrangement with the arena operator.

"This is a 40-year deal and the maintenance [and] the obligations to maintain the arena will be [on] the consortia and the operator," Mr Bleijie said.

"There will be a commercial arrangement going forward with the operators, but as I said, it's over 40 years.

"That will be locked in before the end of the year, before construction starts on the new arena in January."

Brisbane live music stalwarts Lisa and Jess Origliasso — also known as The Veronicas — backed the new arena and said it would be an "incredible opportunity".

"We look around Brisbane and, you know, we have so many memories here — every part of our career has a sentimental attachment to different parts of Brisbane," Jess Origliasso said.

"That is why this is so fantastic — I think this is a dream coming true," Lisa Origliasso said.

The Veronicas described the new area as a "dream coming true". (ABC News: Josh McIntosh)

Developers to be handed Gabba land

Mr Bleijie insisted the government was "not giving away the land" on which the Gabba stands.

"This is a very complicated commercial transaction," he said.

"Part of the process for getting the consortia to design, finance, and operate [the arena] without any government contribution until at least 2031, is to obviously have the ability that they know the investment [is] going forward.

The land the Gabba Stadium stands on will be handed to developers with plans to construct almost 4,000 new homes after 2032. (Supplied)

"We're not giving away the land, it's a commercial transaction and the commercial transaction that we've entered into is over a 40-year period."

He said the state government would be responsible for tearing down the Gabba after the 2032 Games, before handing the land to the consortium.

"The previous government had no plans to unlock this site," he said.

"In contrast, this government does, and we are very happy to partner with the private sector to get things done."

Deputy opposition leader Cameron Dick urged the government to release the details of the deal with Gather Brisbane.

"I think every Queenslander welcomes that this arena's going to go ahead, it's always been part of the Olympics plan," he said.

"But now Queenslanders are paying $600 million for an arena they're not even going to own, with no guarantees — until the government releases the contract details — that they're not going to be the subject of price gouging."

title: Carers of people with disability left exhausted navigating NDIS
text:
Caregivers of people with disabilities say navigating the NDIS to try to get more support for their loved ones is leaving them feeling exhausted and taking a toll on their mental health.

It comes as accessing the NDIS becomes increasingly difficult, after cuts in funding for some sectors began to be rolled out on October 1.

Amanda Solarino, who lives in Romsey just outside Melbourne, is the full-time carer for her 21-year-old son Alex, who is autistic, non‑verbal and has an intellectual disability.

Ms Solarino said she was continuously replacing furniture and fixing walls as a result of her son's escalating aggression, and she struggled to get the help she needed from the NDIS.

Some of the damage caused by Alex at home. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

"Alex's aggression isn't just directed at us or the furniture anymore — he's now turning it on Erica, his 19‑year‑old sister," she said.

"She's so anxious she won't walk down the hallway unless she knows exactly where he is."

Her son's disability also comes at a steep financial cost.

Amanda Solarino lives with several health conditions herself. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

"No one's paying to fix the furniture he breaks ... the $2,000 couch he breaks with his head or the two beds he's broken in the last 18 months," she said.

" The NDIS doesn't pay for ... all the iPads he breaks over his head. "

Ms Solarino said Alex had been kicked out of programmes providing day care in their area, and in a neighbouring town, leaving the family with one support worker who can only come for six hours every Monday.

Ms Solarino has had to plaster the walls after Alex damaged them. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

The stress is affecting Ms Solarino. She has chronic migraine disorder and requires injections every 12 weeks, and her arthritis has worsened.

"They're suspecting autoimmune problems, probably brought on by all the stress," she said.

After Alex's aggression worsened, the NDIS escalated his housing request to crisis level and eventually approved his specialist disability accommodation.

Ms Solarino said the new plan did not fulfil the provisions she had asked for, but she was too exhausted by the process to fight it.

She said all she wanted for Alex was for him to live with some dignity.

"And it's the hardest thing to keep standing up every time you get knocked back," she said.

'Real-world' consequences

On the Sunshine Coast, the family of Breanna Medcalfe, a 24-year-old law student with a spinal injury and quadriplegia, has also faced challenges getting the NDIS help she needs.

Ms Medcalfe is completely paralysed from the neck down and relies on assistance for all activities, including driving and showering.

Breanna Medcalfe now relies on her parents for care. (ABC News: Josh Dye)

Ms Medcalfe has one support worker, but mainly relies on her 60-year-old parents to take care of her daily care responsibilities.

She would like more NDIS-funded support hours, but her requests have been declined.

"Because I have mum and dad and I live at home with them, they are like my informal supports, and they therefore can provide the main support, which is incorrect," she said.

" It's taking a toll on their bodies and their mental health because they have to always be around for me. "

Ms Medcalfe is lodging an appeal against a review of her NDIS plan.

"We haven't yet come to the point where we've run out of support hours, but we've been very restricted as to what we can do," she said.

"Why do we have to justify that we're disabled enough to need this funding?"

Ms Medcalfe says its not right that her parents have to care for her all the time. (ABC News: Josh Dye)

The NDIS refused to answer specific questions about supports provided by family members and the lack of resources in regional areas, referring the ABC to its website.

A spokesperson defended the agency's role in providing "critical, essential services" and confirmed that funding resets for social, economic and community participation and improved daily living supports had gradually rolled out from October 1.

The spokesperson said supports vital to the health, safety, and wellbeing of participants would be excluded from the changes, and added that new safeguards will protect participants with 24-hour care needs.

Ms Medcalfe and her support worker Katy-Lea Holmes. (ABC News: Josh Dye )

Ms Medcalfe says she wants the NDIS to understand the real‑world consequences of its decisions.

"We're not asking for, you know, over the top things," she said.

title: Lambie suggests change to childcare subsidies to cut spending
text:
Independent senator Jacqui Lambie says the government should means-test several subsidies, including child care, as it looks at ways to tighten its budget.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers is facing growing pressure to rein in government expenditure ahead of December's budget update due to cost-of-living pressures, including persistent inflation and a fifth interest rate hike this year.

The Tasmanian senator has suggested one possible lever is to better target government assistance at those who need it most.

"We've got to target better in this country," she told Insiders on Sunday.

She proposed different levels of subsidy for child care depending on income, using a couple with $500,000 income between them as an example.

The ministers who have managed to save money As the government pursues savings "across the board" ahead of the mid-year budget update, an ABC analysis shows only a handful of ministers have managed net savings so far this year.

"Why aren't we means-testing you? Why aren't we doing what we used to do and say, you can have 10 per cent rebate. Not this much rebate," she said.

Asked whether that principle would apply to other subsidies like those on electric vehicles, Senator Lambie said, "Means test it all, why not? That's where you'll get some money from."

The childcare subsidy is already means-tested. Families earning a combined income of about $88,000 get back 90 per cent of fees paid. Government support gradually reduces, with no subsidy available for families who have a combined income above $538,520.

Senator Lambie stressed that she had not seen her constituents under such financial strain since the COVID-19 pandemic, with some turning to putting meat "down their pants and walking out" of supermarkets to feed their children.

"I don't see this financial situation turning around overnight. And I think we've got a couple of more years of it," she said, pointing to uncertainty across several issues like the war in the Middle East.

Gas reservation to face parliament

As politicians return for the final sitting fortnight of the year, the government hopes that it can pass its nationwide gas reservation scheme, which it says will put downward pressure on prices.

The scheme would force liquefied natural gas exporters to keep up to 20 per cent of their product for Australia's domestic market and address consistent threats of shortfalls on the east coast.

Senator Lambie says she will support the legislation when it is debated in the Senate but has called on the government to have "enough courage" to put a 20 per cent tax on export gas.

"Start taking our resources back into our own hands, but we're actually making money off out of them," she said.

The idea is supported by members of the crossbench including the Greens and independent senator David Pocock, who state a 25 per cent tax on gas exports could raise billions of dollars in annual revenue.

The proposal has been repeatedly rejected by the government who argue it needs to protect trade relationships with Asian partners and points to the existing petroleum resources rent tax, which has upwards revisions in forecast revenue.

Shadow Minister for Defence James Paterson said the opposition was concerned about the future of gas investment in Australia as it works constructively with the government, not revealing where it has landed on the gas reservation bill.

"We do want to have more gas here for Australians to access, particularly for industry whose prices have been driven through the roof on Labor's watch," he told Sunday Agenda.

"And we want to see more gas extracted here in Australia. But the government has not done anything to make that easier."

title: Journalist urges federal government to intervene in NT 'social catastrophe'
text:
A veteran ABC journalist has delivered a searing analysis of Northern Territory politics in a new book that chronicles how government policies have worsened life outcomes for Aboriginal people in the NT.

Murray McLaughlin's new book is out now. (Supplied)

In his new book The Northern Territory: A Litany of Failure, Murray McLaughlin — who worked as an ABC TV current affairs journalist and later as an adviser to the Northern Land Council (NLC) — argues the federal government has been mostly passively complicit in the welfare of the Territory's Aboriginal citizens declining over five decades.

As well as a critique of failure, the book serves as an appeal to the federal government to intervene in a territory McLaughlin describes as a "beguiling and bewitching place, a unique wonderland".

He writes:

"While Canberra's reluctance to dictate prevails, one certainty remains: the Territory will never right itself. "A mendicant jurisdiction beholden to the Commonwealth is allowed to bring embarrassment and shame upon the whole country with policy agendas that disproportionately impact on Aboriginal people while it lavishes benefits on the non-Aboriginal population."

He says the Albanese government "has done little to avert the social catastrophe unravelling before its eyes".

"As Canberra pours billions of dollars into the Territory to shore up northern defence systems and the petrochemical industry prepares to prosper from the bountiful gas fields to be fracked in the immense Beetaloo Basin south-east of Darwin, housing, health and education markers continue to deteriorate for the Territory's Aboriginal population, especially those living in remote communities."

Patrick Dodson wrote the foreword to The Northern Territory: A Litany of Failure. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

In the book's foreword, former Labor senator Patrick Dodson, for whom McLaughlin worked as an adviser, reinforces its central message: That the NT's self-government in place since 1978 has been "a failed experiment" which has hastened "a collapse of social order".

But Mr Dodson writes that he and McLaughlin share hope that the Commonwealth will use "a rare political window … to show leadership and imagination in rebuilding the Territory and redirecting its troubled course".

Land rights under attack, Intervention 'cataclysmic'

Much of the book's conversational, accessible political history of the Territory is told from McLaughlin's firsthand reporting experience, and then from the sidelines of fights between the NLC and NT governments on policies affecting the rights of Aboriginal people.

He takes readers on an evocative journey through the Territory, analysing the policy blows Country Liberal Party (CLP) and Labor governments have delivered to Aboriginal people, focusing particularly on how successive CLP governments, aided at times by Canberra Coalition administrations, have tried to erode federal NT Aboriginal land rights laws.

The book claims successive governments from both major parties have failed Aboriginal people in the NT. (Torsten Blackwood, AFP)

He writes the Territory's first CLP chief minister Paul Everingham's 1978 administration opposed Aboriginal land rights and "ruthlessly" challenged almost every land claim.

This continued through to the 2013 CLP Adam Giles administration, McLaughlin writes, as they tried to persuade the Commonwealth to hand control of the land rights law to them.

McLaughlin documents how "Aboriginal incarceration rates have grown exponentially", starting with 1995 CLP chief minister Shane Stone's administration introducing mandatory sentencing for a range of offences.

"The law, predictably, had a disproportionate impact on Aboriginal people, and its impact had been cynically calculated," he writes.

The book also chronicles a series of Labor government policies during the early 2000s that harmed Aboriginal interests, including the 2001 Clare Martin administration's approval for Xstrata to dig through a sacred site to expand its McArthur River Mine in 2006.

The book uses the approval to destroy a sacred site at the McArthur River Mine as an example of how governments have ignored Aboriginal interests. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

McLaughlin labels this as "a conspicuous example of how governments have brutally brushed aside Aboriginal interests when development proposals take priority".

He writes how the following 2007 Paul Henderson Labor administration wound back bilingual education in Aboriginal community schools, concentrated government funding into larger Indigenous communities and amalgamated 53 remote local government councils into eight "super shires".

"Worse, the resultant changes coincided with the Howard government's Intervention, with communities never recovering from that double calamity," he writes.

McLaughlin analyses how both a "flawed" ABC Lateline story about an alleged paedophile ring in Central Australia and Clare Martin's "failure to respond with boldness and urgency to the Little Children Are Sacred report" resulted in the NT National Emergency Response — the Intervention.

John Howard and his Indigenous affairs minister Mal Brough launched the Intervention, with Mr Brough visiting Mutujulu in 2007. (Ian Waldie, file photo: Getty Images)

Seventy-three communities were identified as primary sites for intervention and the army and police were brought in from other jurisdictions.

"The scope of the Intervention was extraordinary and its impact on Aboriginal people cataclysmic," he writes. "Although Aboriginal men were offended because the Intervention had branded them child molesters and, as traditional owners, they felt threatened about the Commonwealth's compulsory leasing of community lands, the most troubling policy … was compulsory income management, facilitated by the suspension of the Racial Discrimination Act 1975. "Federal Labor, not wanting to be wedged, embraced the Intervention."

Treatment of youth detainees scrutinised

The 2013 Adam Giles government's treatment of youth prisoners, including the use of tear gas, mechanical restraints, spit hoods and indefinite detention isolation, that was exposed by the ABC is scrutinised in the book.

Youth detainees were shackled and hooded the day after tear gas was used on them at Don Dale. (Supplied)

"The brutalisation of children and their bastardisation in detention were painfully illustrated by the treatment of a 14-year-old Aboriginal boy, whose explosive behaviour on 21 August 2014 precipitated the tear-gassing of him and other detainees," McLaughlin writes.

McLaughlin analyses how the 2016 administration of Labor's Michael Gunner — summed up as "an uninspiring and shallow chief minister who promised plenty but delivered little" — "slithered and dithered" over recommendations of the royal commission into youth justice abuse.

He writes that Mr Gunner toughened bail laws "in the full knowledge that incarceration rates, especially of Aboriginal people, would blow out beyond already record-breaking numbers, and his commitment to a treaty began to fade".

Murray McLaughlin describes Michael Gunner as "an uninspiring and shallow chief minister". (ABC News: Che Chorley)

McLaughlin also accuses the Gunner government of attacking Aboriginal land rights by passing laws making it easier for pastoralists to develop cattle stations for other uses without native title holders having to be consulted or compensated.

"Gunner's government would soon resort to drawing from the same well of prejudice against Aboriginal land claims as had nourished the Country Liberal Party," he writes.

The veteran journalist follows the NT right up to the current CLP government, documenting how Indigenous incarceration continued to dramatically increase with tightened bail laws following the 2023 murder of a bottle shop worker, Declan Laverty.

"By August 2025, the government was boasting that more than 3,300 people had been refused bail, a 44 per cent increase over the same period in 2024," the books reads.

'Things are deadly serious'

McLaughlin's chronicle finishes with current Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro's appointment of former NT Cattlemen's Association President David Connolly earlier this year, and her determined defence of that after racist social media posts he had previously made were exposed.

Territorians protested David Connolly's appointment as administrator earlier this year. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"Obduracy and disdain for proper process marked Finocchiaro's announcement," he writes. "Albanese's refusal … to reject the Territory government's egregious recommendation of a man with a record of racist commentary to be the Territory's Administrator … spoke of a deliberate avoidance of responsibility."

McLaughlin told the ABC he hoped the federal government was starting to understand that the Territory's Aboriginal people were facing a crisis so severe that it must now intervene.

Despite its 'litany of failure', Murray McLaughlin is hopeful the federal government will intervene.

"The Commonwealth has got to recognise that it's got responsibilities here," he said.

"It's going to take something like a Marshall Plan to just catch up.

"Something has to happen — these remote communities are on their knees.

"[Independent NT politician] Yingiya Guyula said it when he resigned, that Aboriginal culture is being destroyed in front of our eyes.

"Things are deadly serious."

title: Swimming stars tipped for big 2027 despite illness, injury hiccups
text:
Battered by illness and injury, a trio of Australian Olympic swimming stars are being backed to be ready for Los Angeles Games.

Between them, Kaylee McKeown, Mollie O'Callaghan and Kyle Chalmers have won 11 Olympic gold medals.

McKeown returned to competition over the weekend at the inaugural Swim GP in Melbourne, having not raced since last year because of glandular fever.

Chalmers was poolside at the event, in the midst of a six-week break from swimming as he manages long-term back problems.

O'Callaghan, who nursed back and shoulder injuries through the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, was a late withdrawal from the Swim GP because of a skin infection.

McKeown said the one positive of her illness was that it had happened this year, not next.

Australian swimming head coach Rohan Taylor echoed that sentiment about the three stars in the context of the four-year Olympic cycle.

Mollie O'Callaghan missed competing at Swim GP due to an infection. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"No-one will remember what happens in 2026 [in terms of injury or illness]. You can't worry about that now," Taylor told AAP.

"You have to get them right, you have to remember their talent won't go anywhere.

"It's about getting them healthy and then letting the fitness build. We know they can race and we just have to get ourselves to the arena fit and healthy, then we will be right."

McKeown made a successful return to racing at the Swim GP and Taylor was pleased with the backstroke queen's progress after the illness knocked her flat.

"I live on the Sunshine Coast, so I get to see it up close and see the progression," Taylor said.

"It's really good to see her back racing. She's such a competitor.

"She just looked back to her normal self, competitive, focused when the race was on, but enjoying herself.

"She just has to build momentum back."

McKeown gave a glimpse of her blistering backstroke speed on Saturday night, storming home after the staggered start to beat Ella Ramsay's breaststroke in the 50m skins champions race.

It was her first racing since the world championships in July last year.

Kaylee McKeown is one of Australian swimming's biggest stars. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"I've been doing some pretty solid sessions, but it's hard to come into these races — not racing all year — and then my body just hasn't recovered as quickly as it would," McKeown said.

"It's good, nice practice and gives a bit of confidence that I'm still swimming well.

"It's great there are no times, which takes the pressure off. It's just about racing."

As McKeown notes, glandular fever affects people differently and in her case, "it just really knocked me flat".

So competing for the Tsunami team at the Swim GP, with nothing riding on the results, was an ideal stepping stone as McKeown looks to next year's world championships and then the 2028 Olympics.

"It's really good fun and I'm glad we can race in this format," she said.

"It's taken a long time to build back and then I have to build to where I was, which is even more of a gap.

"I'm lucky it was this year and not next year, when it counts, so it's a blessing in disguise. I've had some nice time at home."

Swim GP is a points-based competition in a 25m pool, with no official times recorded and a variety of relay and individual race formats.

The Wahoo team, lead by Meg Harris and Sam Short, dominated the two-night Swim GP and comfortably won on 222 points.

McKeown's Tsunami were next on 173, ahead of Kraken (170) and KingTide (149).

AAP

Former Australian bowler Chadd Sayers has blown the sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal wide open, backing Usman Khawaja’s assertion that the whole Australian Test cricket squad in South Africa in 2018 knew of the plot to scratch the match ball and that they started doing it in the Port Elizabeth Test – one game before Cameron Bancroft was caught in Cape Town. “I’m pretty confident to say that everyone knew,” Sayers told radio station SEN, for whom he commentated Sunday’s one-day international between Australia and England. Chadd Sayers made his Test debut for Australia in Johannesburg in 2018, in a team depleted by the suspensions to Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft. Getty Images Sayers, who did not play in Port Elizabeth — now Gqeberha — or Cape Town but made his debut in the following Test in Johannesburg also revealed that, as a fringe player in the squad, he came onto the field with drinks at a break in play earlier in that series and collected sandpaper from Bancroft and disposed of it. He said that happened before TV cameras caught Bancroft trying to conceal sandpaper down his pants in Cape Town. “[The sandpaper] was given to me to take off. That wasn’t planned or anything. I was just the player who took the drinks out at the time. I recall it was a wicket or a drinks break after tea,” Sayers said.

Asked when he became aware during that series that sandpaper was being used on the ball, Sayers replied: “In Port Elizabeth … it was used in two Test matches, and there were discussions in change rooms of how we were going get the ball to reverse and what was going to be used ... there was numerous conversations of it around the change rooms.” He said, like Bancroft, he was a young player trying to fit into the Australian side at the time. Chadd Sayers recalled his memories of the sandpaper scandal for SEN listeners on Sunday. It is difficult for young NRL players of Pasifika or New Zealand heritage who are expected to carry a torch for the family but at the same time hold ambitions to step away from their shadow. Changed eligibility rules have thrown up multiple challenges, including threats to the future of the Kangaroos, who play the Kiwis in the World Cup final on Sunday. Passion: Tonga’s Robert Toia. Getty Images Consider the case of 22-year-old Roosters premiership player Robert Toia, who represented Queensland and Tonga this year. Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters received a long text from the young centre late on the day before the NRL grand final, in which Toia declared his World Cup allegiance to Tonga – reneging on an earlier undertaking to Walters to represent Australia if selected. Walters was disappointed with Toia’s decision, particularly because it followed the defection days earlier of Titans and Maroons winger Jojo Fifita to Tonga in the World Cup. However, he understood that Toia, with a grand final to play the following day, wanted to clear his mind of the competing loyalties and the family pressure.

Advertisement

“I don’t hold any grudges,” says Walters. “They need to go where their heart is. I said that to both of them. There is a lot of pressure from their Polynesian families. But that’s OK. They are just doing what is best for them.” The passion of many NRL players, like Melbourne’s Eli Katoa, for their ancestral homelands, such as Tonga and Samoa, is almost endemic, while others face relentless pressure from their extended family to represent the land of their fathers – despite the pay disparity of $850 per game compared with the Kangaroos receiving $40,000 for the tournament. Loading New International Rugby League board eligibility rules will allow more players like Toia to elect to play for countries other than Australia. Under the rules in place for this year’s World Cup, players are eligible to be selected by the country where one of their grandparents was born. But the IRLB this week extended the criteria to cover the birthplaces of eight great-grandparents, meaning the supply of NRL players to Pacific countries competing in future World Cups will cover the next generation of players. Casey McLean, a 20-year-old centre, was born in Blacktown, plays for Penrith, represented NSW in Origin this year and will play for New Zealand in Sunday’s World Cup final. As the number of homegrown players of Pasifika and New Zealand heritage approximates half the NRL population, the eligibility rules both ensure the best players are available for the code’s big money earner, State of Origin, while also making international rugby league more competitive and therefore more lucrative in terms of TV rights.

Advertisement

The rules, however, run the risk of redistributing NRL talent among the World Cup countries, rather than growing it at both grassroots level in the emerging countries and in Australia itself. As players in the NRL increasingly commit to New Zealand, Tonga, Samoa, Fiji and England, the numbers in the pool available for the Kangaroos diminishes. The NRL threatens to become the English Premier League, whose riches attract the world’s best soccer players, reducing the availability of positions for players of English background. Significantly, England has not won a FIFA World Cup since 1966. Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters is concerned the number of Australian eligible players will decline. Getty Images Walters recognises the development problem ahead. “We need to have more avenues for players eligible only for Australia,” he says. “We need Australia to develop big forwards and probably wingers as well. The Polynesian players develop a bit quicker than the guys of Australian heritage only.” Pointing to the size difference at junior levels, he adds: “We also need to ensure Australian kids stay in the game.”

Advertisement

Walters concedes this year’s World Cup exposed the Kangaroos’ lack of depth in middle forwards. Australia’s starting props against Samoa in the World Cup semi-final were Tino Fa’asuamaleaui, who represented Samoa at the 2019 tournament, and Keaon Koloamatangi, who played for Tonga at the 2022 iteration. Both switched their allegiance to Australia and were desperately needed in the early clashes against Samoa. As it transpired, with Patrick Carrigan coming off the bench and running 163 metres, Australia won the battle up front. “We won the middle metres,” says Walters. “It was a real focus for us and will be in the final against New Zealand, with their big pack.” Related Article Exclusive

Rugby League World Cup ‘All I want to do is put the red jersey on’: Eli Katoa’s road to recovery The IRLB has not yet resolved whether to categorise Tonga and Samoa as Tier 1 countries, which would require players to commit to them permanently. A 12-month grace period is being considered, allowing players to finally declare their permanent allegiance. It also allows the board time to consider whether there are any unintended consequences of the changed eligibility rules. Toia was born in Auckland but moved with his large family to Brisbane at age six. Toia agonised over his decision to play for Tonga before informing Walters. He may now be required to choose again.

Advertisement

The IRLB must question whether they are exerting too much stress on young players who are already besieged by pressure from their extended families. Some may choose not to play at all. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday. Sign up for our Sport newsletter.

It was the latest twist in weeks of violent reversals, with oil prices surging before dipping, bond yields lurching and the sudden downfall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang shaking one of the bull market’s biggest bets. Inflation fears keep upending bets on the US Federal Reserve tensions with Iran won’t stop jolting oil prices, and confidence in the AI boom remains shaky. Peter Morgan Beneath the relative resilience of major stock benchmarks, the difference between a windfall and a painful loss has often come down to market timing. The S&P 500 has moved an average of 1.6 per cent a day so far in November and the Nasdaq 100 an even more bruising 2.4 per cent, the largest average daily moves for both since the tariff turmoil of April 2025. Bonds have offered little refuge. The two-year Treasury yield had climbed nearly 28 basis points this month before Friday’s retreat, following similarly large moves in opposite directions over the previous two months. A popular long-term Treasury ETF has endured its own reversals, while volatility in an iShares fund tracking the classic 60/40 stock-and-bond portfolio has jumped. Professional trend-followers have been wrong-footed, suffering their biggest drawdown of the year.

Advertisement

Driving the tumult: inflation fears keep upending bets on the Fed, tensions with Iran won’t stop jolting oil prices, and confidence in the AI boom remains shaky. Related Article Aviation Inside Boeing’s mission to rebuild trust in the 737 after years of turbulence For Chris Davis, chairman of Davis Advisors, the unsettling part is how readily investors seem to be shrugging it all off. “The uncertainty is enormous, the fragility, the things that can go wrong very suddenly, enormous – combined with a tremendous amount of complacency in the market,” he said. Investors are embracing two distinct playbooks: buying the whole market through tried-and-tested index funds, or doubling down on the kind of speculative wagers that have delivered both spectacular gains and crushing losses this year. Vanguard’s flagship S&P 500 fund attracted nearly $US24 billion ($35.5 billion) in October, while a triple-leveraged semiconductor ETF pulled in $US9 billion despite losing half its value. Even as Nvidia’s upheaval rattles the artificial intelligence trade, demand for Anthropic’s planned blockbuster initial public offering has exceeded the shares available several times over.

Advertisement

The S&P 500, with a 2.5 per cent rally, staged its first weekly advance since early October, even as just a small group of its members is trading at their 52-week highs. The Nasdaq 100 added 3.5 per cent in the five-day stretch. For some professional investors, the message from the bond market is reason enough to stay cautious. Skyler Weinand, chief investment officer of the $US4.5 billion shop Regan Capital in Dallas, says 10-year Treasury yields could stay above 5 per cent for the foreseeable future, and the Federal Reserve will continue to increase interest rates. “We are staying in higher-quality, defensive names that aren’t taking on additional debt and are producing ample cash flows,” he said. “We are in the same camp of running minimal leverage and staying defensive until we see better downstream gains from AI.” Retail buyers have poured tens of billions of dollars into equity funds over the past two weeks. They’ve also been snapping up leveraged funds after sharp declines in assets at the start of November, raising the possibility that dip buying could help stabilise the battered technology trade. Among the more aggressive wagers, a group of double-leveraged Nvidia ETFs have attracted roughly $US900 million over the past week, even as the chipmaker’s shares lost 13 per cent following the departure of its longtime chief executive officer.
