For Joseph Crow, a 35-year-old retail investor from Connecticut, the turmoil offered a chance for a quick payday. On Tuesday, he says he wagered $US3000 on call options expiring in three days on the triple-levered Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF (SOXL), betting on a fast rebound in chip stocks. The conviction paid off the next day — Crow says he sold for roughly $US23,000. Related Article Executive shake-up ‘I don’t care’: Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO “It was definitely a lotto purchase,” he said. “Seeing Nvidia so beaten down, it was like, ‘Man, something’s gotta lift eventually.’” For all the money chasing quick fortunes, the familiar index funds continue to exert a powerful pull. Vanguard’s VOO and VTI, iShares’ IVV, State Street’s SPY and SPYM and Invesco’s QQQ have captured about 30 per cent of all equity ETF flows this year, a share that’s been rising sharply since 2023, according to Athanasios Psarofagis at Bloomberg Intelligence. VOO alone has absorbed about $140 billion in 2026, a sum that puts it on pace for a record annual inflow. All told, the market’s violent swings have created booms and busts for those trying to ride them, while reinforcing the appeal of a simpler approach: owning the market rather than trying to pick winners and losers.

Budapest: Hungarian authorities have recovered nearly $30 million in cash, some buried in forests or hidden in farm buildings and warehouses, in a bribery investigation into Miklos Sesztak, a minister under former leader Viktor Orban. Prime Minister Peter Magyar ousted Orban after 16 years in power in an April election, pledging to mend ties with the European Union strained by years of disagreements under Orban, and to launch a sweeping investigation into allegations of graft. Stacks of forints (Hungarian currency) in a video from the anti-corruption National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Finance Minister Andras Karman said it took a dozen state treasury workers eight hours – using banknote counters – to count the cash that had been retrieved. Magyar said the recovered cash signalled the end of what he described as a “mafia” led by Orban’s right-wing Fidesz party and his Christian Democrat allies during Orban’s rule. Fidesz wrote in a Facebook post that it hoped Sesztak was not connected to the cash. “Since the change of regime, every lawmaker in Hungary has sworn an oath to abide by and enforce the law. Fidesz-KDNP (Christian Democrats) cannot associate itself with anyone who fails to do so. We trust that the images published by the NVVH [asset recovery office] have nothing to do with Miklos Sesztak,” Fidesz wrote. This Democrat wants to change that James Massola November 15, 2026 — 1:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Washington, DC: Australia should be given priority access to the most capable artificial intelligence tools developed in the US and the Trump administration was wrong to temporarily withhold access to the powerful Claude Mythos tool. That’s the view of Lori Trahan, the Democratic congresswoman for Massachusetts, helping to lead a push for more stringent regulation of AI in the US. Lori Trahan, Democratic congresswoman for Massachusetts. Bloomberg She believes that as part of the push for better “rules of the road” to ensure the technology is properly controlled, the US should also foster more open collaboration with its Five Eyes intelligence partners, particularly Australia and the UK. “Innovation and safety are not at odds with each other, and I think we should just remind ourselves that when we set those standards high, we bring the rest of the world with us. But that’s also incumbent on our collaboration with our allies,” she said.

Advertisement

In April, Anthropic released its Claude Mythos AI model, which is particularly skillful at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in IT systems. Australian government security agencies and even Australian citizens working on AI in the US – along with all other foreign nationals – were initially barred from working with Mythos after a Trump administration edict, which was partly wound back after a couple of months. Claude Mythos was developed by Anthropic. Bloomberg Anthropic, which makes the Claude AI chatbot and is on the verge of a record $USD1.4 trillion initial public offer, has heavily restricted access to Mythos to financial institutions, major tech companies and cloud services providers like Amazon. Trahan, who is a member of Congress’ House Committee on Energy and Commerce, told this masthead the technology should not have been withheld from Five Eyes intelligence partners. “We rely on those relationships with our allies, and so I think that there’s a collaboration that we need to strike. In fact, we should have a Western stack [a collection of software tools] that is unified and fostering collaboration,” she said.

Advertisement

Anthropic says it wants to train its popular Claude models in Australia. Bloomberg Speaking at the Takeoff AI conference in Washington DC, Trahan said “there’s no question that AI was on the ballot” during the recent mid-term elections and that exit polls showed “that AI mattered in the congressional races”. There is a growing push in the United States for greater AI regulation and safeguards and Trahan, working alongside California Republican Jay Obernolte to achieve bipartisan reforms, has helped lead the way. The Australian government recently announced an AI Safety Institute in response to a push for greater regulation of artificial intelligence domestically, something which has been anathema to the Trump administration. Trahan thinks the position of the Trump administration could shift now the Democrats have a majority in Congress. “You never know what deal the president will sign,” she said.

Advertisement

David Wroe, director of AI security the organisation Good Ancestors, welcomed Trahan’s comments and said Mythos had the power to “carry out any cyber activity you can imagine”. “Obviously, we want Australia to be first in line to have access to the most advanced US technology, but I understand why US companies and government want to be careful about who has access, given how powerful they are becoming,” he said. “Lori is right to say we need to spread risks, the US needs to look at building infrastructure in other trusted countries, and it is very much in Australia’s interest to have that done in Australia.” Australia is one of a handful of countries being examined by Anthropic as a second location to set up AI training data centres, which are more powerful than centres that simply answer users’ questions to chatbots. Training centres can be located more remotely from major population centres but the question of what the most advanced models train, and compensation for copyright holders in Australia and overseas, remains unresolved. title: Nvidia’s Huang is not alone. Here are some of the costliest affairs in history
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the words of the normally sombre Economist magazine, it could go down as “the most expensive shag in history”. Following Nvidia boss Jensen Huang’s admission of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, some $US500 billion ($738 billion) has been wiped from the value of his AI firm. Speculation is also growing that his wife, Lori, may file for divorce following claims he had a second affair with a married employee. If she does so, she could be in line for a $75 billion payout – making her one of the world’s richest women and leaving Huang to rue some of the costliest infidelity ever. Yet a glance at history shows that he is not alone – as business leaders, politicians, sportsmen and kings have all learnt the hard way … Jeff Bezos and MacKenzie Scott divorced in 2019. Scott was left with a 4 per cent stake valued at about $US38 billion at the time of the divorce. AP Prime spot for price In terms of sheer, eye-watering expense, the costliest affair in history was conducted by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. Then the world’s richest man, Bezos began a secret romance with Lauren Sanchez, a married former Fox News presenter, in early 2018. It didn’t stay secret for long. The following year the National Enquirer published lurid details of his romance with Sanchez, including private text messages. Bezos and his wife, MacKenzie Scott, divorced six months later, with her receiving 4 per cent of Amazon stock, valued then at $56 billion. It remains one of the largest divorce settlements in history. Tiger Woods and then-fiancee Elin Nordegren. Detroit Free Press Woods in the rough In 2009, golfer Tiger Woods seemingly had the world at his feet – both on and off the course. With 14 major championships under his belt and a string of lucrative sponsorships, he had become the first sportsman ever to earn more than $US1 billon. Meanwhile, his marriage to his Swedish wife, Elin Nordegren, seemed the very picture of domestic bliss. Then, that November, reports emerged of an affair with a former New York nightclub hostess, Rachel Uchitel. Two days later, after a late-night confrontation with his wife, a shoeless, dishevelled Woods drove off at speed from his house, only to crash into a tree in a neighbour’s garden. Numerous other women came forward claiming infidelity with the golfer, whose subsequent divorce settlement was said to be worth hundreds of millions. The scandal also cost him vast amounts in cancelled sponsorship deals and affected his game. It was not until 2019 that he won another major trophy.

Advertisement

That footage of Andy Byron and Kristin Cabot at a Coldplay concert. TikTok Kiss-cam cost Few affairs have been exposed in such toe-curlingly embarrassing fashion as the one between US tech-firm boss Andy Byron and his employee Kristin Cabot. Last year the pair went to a Coldplay concert near Boston, enjoying complimentary VIP balcony seats. Unfortunately, a live feed of the concert on a big screen then panned to the happy couple just as they enjoyed a romantic clinch. “Either they’re having an affair or they’re just very shy,” remarked Coldplay’s Chris Martin as Cabot tried to cover her face while Byron ducked out of sight. Footage of the clip quickly went viral, and while the pair later denied that it was technically an affair – both were separating from their partners at the time – each quit the tech firm, Astronomer, shortly afterwards. As the company’s HR director at the time of the incident, Cabot should perhaps have known better than to mix business with pleasure. Yet as a result of “Coldplaygate” she received a stream of online abuse calling her a “home-wrecker” and later complained of being rendered unemployable. “I became a meme, I was the most maligned HR manager in HR history,” she said. David Petraeus, then commander of the NATO International Security Assistance Force, with Paula Broadwell, his biographer, in Afghanistan in 2011. NYT Warrior Monk with a wandering eye During America’s 20-year War on Terror, General David Petraeus was the man the White House turned to at the (not infrequent) moments it all went pear-shaped. Venerated for his thoughtful hearts-and-minds policies, the “Warrior Monk” masterminded two successful “troop surges”, in Iraq and Afghanistan, and in 2011 was appointed director of the CIA. Then, just as he was being tipped as a future Republican presidential candidate, news broke of an extramarital affair between him and his biographer, Paula Broadwell. He promptly resigned, and in 2015 was also fined $US100,000 ($148,000) for passing Broadwell classified information. His rumoured presidential bid never happened. Instead, the 2016 Republican candidate was one Donald J. Trump. Gary Hart and Donna Rice in 1987. Getty Images

Advertisement

Too much monkey business In the 1980s, Colorado senator Gary Hart was considered one of the Democrats’ best prospects since John F. Kennedy. Charismatic, Yale-educated and handsome, he quickly emerged as the frontrunner for the party’s nomination for 1988’s presidential election. Yet despite being hailed as the leader of a new generation, he expected the United States’ media to observe old-school rules about not reporting politicians’ private indiscretions. Times, however, had changed, and in May that year the National Enquirer published pictures of Hart on a yacht with Donna Rice, a woman 20 years his junior, sitting on his lap. It didn’t help that Hart was wearing a T-shirt named after the vessel, which was called Monkey Business. He then withdrew from the presidential race, which was won by Republican George H. W. Bush. John Profumo leaves the War Office with his wife Valerie Hobson in 1963 as he prepared to make a statement at the House of Commons about his affair with Christine Keeler. PA Images via Getty Images Never had it so bad … What was arguably the most notorious fling in modern Britain began in 1961, when John Profumo, the Harrow-educated secretary of state for war in Harold Macmillan’s administration, met 19-year-old model Christine Keeler at a society party at Cliveden House, the seat of Viscount Astor. Profumo – a friend of Queen Elizabeth II – then embarked on an affair with Keeler, yet denied any impropriety in a statement in the House of Commons two years later. Christine Keeler in her London flat in 1963. Mirrorpix via Getty Images A police investigation then proved he had lied, while Keeler later claimed to have also been sleeping with Yevgeny Ivanov, a Soviet naval attache at Moscow’s London embassy. Profumo resigned in disgrace, living the rest of his life in near-anonymity as a charity worker in the East End. But the real damage done was to the ruling class that he embodied. The scandal not only torpedoed the credibility of the conservative government under Macmillan, it hastened the end of traditional “deference” towards “establishment” authority.

Advertisement

Peter and Catherine of Russia in 1756. Anna Rosina de Gasc, Getty Images Lover of the Russian queen Unhappy in her loveless, sexless arranged marriage to grand duke Peter of Russia, the future Catherine the Great embarked on a passionate affair with Stanisław Poniatowski – a tall, handsome Polish nobleman. With tongues wagging in the Moscow court, he was eventually banished, while Peter ascended the throne as emperor. The two lovers, however, stayed in touch, and when Catherine then became empress after her husband’s death, she helped install Poniatowski as king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania. Her support was more about geopolitics than a gesture of affection, however, and quickly backfired. Far from being a compliant Moscow pawn, Poniatowski then tried to shift his kingdom away from Russia’s influence, forcing Catherine to send in Russian troops. After a series of occupations and partitions, Poniatowski was forced to abdicate his throne in 1795, and the Polish-Lithuanian kingdom ceased to exist. The first meeting of Tudor king Henry VIII and his ill-fated wife Anne Boleyn, as imagined by painter Daniel Maclise in 1835. Getty Images A courtly affair In medieval times the British royal family did not generally have to worry much about media scandal: newspapers hadn’t been invented, and gossipy courtiers could quickly be hauled off to the Tower. Henry VIII, however, did have to suffer Pope Clement VII, in Rome, who refused to sanction his marriage to Anne Boleyn after his previous one to Catherine of Aragon failed to produce an heir. Facing excommunication, Henry secretly married Boleyn in 1533 anyway while still legally married to Aragon – an act of bigamy in Rome’s eyes. He then severed ties with the Catholic Church. It put Britain on the path to Protestantism, scientific advance and prosperity but also led to bloody internal conflict with Catholics and the English Civil War. Poor Boleyn was also later executed. title: US aviation shutdown may have been due to a faulty router, Trump admin says
text:
In brief The halt was declared after upgrade work on an old copper wire caused "issues" with communication with airplanes.

The ground stop raised serious concerns about the country's ageing infrastructure.

A massive, nearly five-hour shutdown of the US aviation system that disrupted more than 20,000 flights may have been the fault of a single router installed by government contractor L3Harris.

The incident is the latest painful example of the ageing US air traffic control ‌telecom system and the struggles to replace systems while keeping the old communications working.

In recent years, the Federal Aviation Administration's ageing systems have failed after errant fibre cuts, accidental file deletions, and a strong chemical smell caused by a melted component. The system will fail again until it is properly upgraded, government officials said.

"This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment," US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said ‌on Sunday AEDT.

Duffy said on Friday L3Harris was conducting routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fibre at at least one remote location.

Officials told Reuters news agency there may have been problems with routers installed in both Arkansas and Texas.

"We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said.

L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and was "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop ‌of our nation's air travel".

L3 ‌noted it has completed more ⁠than 70 per cent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fibre-optic system.

The FAA spends $US1 billion ($1.5 billion) annually to maintain its old copper wire system and is racing to replace it with more modern fibre-based communications.

"We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job," Duffy said, noting that "virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fibre, from analog to digital".

The issue began overloading communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centres across the country, which prompted the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop because it could not identify a root cause.

Duffy said the new routers started flooding other routers with over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, which sparked ⁠communications issues with planes and radar at FAA facilities.

US transportation secretary Sean Duffy says the federal aviation authority hadn't yet determined the cause of the fault. Source: AP / Tom Brenner

Bedford said the FAA had to take the action ‌when it lost "the ability for those routers to communicate data". The FAA is still trying to understand the root cause of what went wrong.

The FAA said communications did not go down but led to instability in data at ‌the centres. It did not lead to centres going dark. The routers being replaced are about 25 years old, Duffy said, and were supposed to be replaced in 2006.

Small mishaps leading to catastrophic consequences are not new to the US air traffic control network. A 2023 FAA nationwide ground stop that lasted 90 minutes and disrupted 11,000 flights was caused by a government contractor unintentionally deleting files.

That led to the first nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks.

Friday's outage hit as a surge in travellers began weekend travel.

The FAA got $US12.5 billion ($18.5 billion) to ‌upgrade its badly ageing air traffic control and telecom system from the US Congress, and Duffy has asked for $US50 billion ($74 billion) more for air traffic control and airports.

A teenage pop star from the Philippines won the first Asia edition of Eurovision overnight after a night of power ballads, pop-dance hits and pyrotechnics from the makers of the cult European kitsch fest.

title: Why Australians could face cyber security risks in the wake of the Microsoft outage
text:
In Brief Organisations scrambling to keep working during the outage may have caused a major cybersecurity risk, experts say.

About 79 per cent of Australian consumers want stronger protections for online services.

Australia's peak cyber security body fears an enormous amount of sensitive information may have bypassed normal security walls during a day-long Microsoft outage.

Global disruption of the company's Outlook and Teams finally eased on Saturday after about 24 hours of chaos that crippled online communications.

The mass outage forced some ‌organisations to revert to fax and halted at least one European bond repurchase.

Described as a disaster for the Australian business sector, it has deepened questions about global reliance on a handful of major tech companies supplying essential software and the cloud infrastructure underpinning it.

The Australian Information Security Association (AISA) said organisations scrambling to keep working during the outage using personal email accounts, USB drives and other alternative platforms may have caused a major cybersecurity risk.

"When people can't access the systems they rely on, they find ways to keep working," AISA board director Doctor Rajiv Shah said.

"Given the massive number of organisations affected around the world, we could be looking at an enormous amount of information that has moved outside normal security arrangements in a single day," he said.

"We need to understand how much additional cyber risk has been created."

Billions potentially lost

It mounts more pressure on Australian businesses feared to have lost billions of dollars within only 12 hours of the shutdown, according to Ashwin Pal from accounting firm RSM Australia.

"That's not just direct but indirect costs as well," he said.

"A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel's back for smaller entities."

He said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans but many businesses didn't have a fallback.

"They're just at a standstill — if you don't actually have a plan B, then you've got a problem," he said.

Shah said businesses needed to build greater redundancy, such as independent communication channels, offline access to critical information and alternative ways to authenticate users in case of a major outage.

The Australian Computer Society renewed its call for a national review of sovereign risk in Australian IT, whilst Australian consumer groups said the outage highlighted a need for stronger complaints systems.

"Australians who couldn't get paid, couldn't send an invoice or couldn't reach a government service are entitled to be worried," chief executive of Computer Society Prins Ralston said.

"Where were the direct updates to Australian customers and media — and who will answer for the lost productivity and the cost to the economy?"

According to research by the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network, consumer trust in big tech is at an all time low with many feeling trapped using platforms they find hard to move from.

About 79 per cent of consumers want stronger protections for online services while 81 per cent say the apps they use are important to their day-to-day life.

title: The science behind Anthony Albanese's unusual hot mic moment
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen were overheard discussing concerns about the impact of phones on health.

Researchers have examined the effects of electromagnetic radiation on human organs.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was caught on a hot mic joking with Energy Minister Chris Bowen about phone radiation and penises at the COP31 climate summit.

The prime minister was recorded speaking to Bowen on Friday evening as they waited for a roundtable discussion to begin in Antalya, Türkiye.

"Do you keep your phone here? Don't," Albanese cautioned Bowen, gesturing to his left breast pocket, sparking an exchange about the potential impact of mobile phones on the body, including the heart's rhythm.

"I'm more conscious ... I've stopped putting it in my pants pocket," Bowen began before Albanese interrupted.

"Because of your d--k," the prime minister said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It's rather important — arguably more important than the heart," Bowen replied as the pair laughed.

Channel Seven initially broadcast a clip of their private banter on Friday evening.

A spokesperson for Albanese downplayed the leaked moment, saying the pair "were having a joke in between meetings," according to Nine newspapers.

However, the joking exchange raises questions about the impact of mobile phones on health, including common concerns they can cause cancer.

Can phones affect your organs and health?

A large number of studies have investigated these links, with some studies raising concerns and others finding little convincing evidence of harm.

The current available research does not indicate using a mobile phone is associated with harmful health effects, according to the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA).

Mobile phones emit radiofrequency electromagnetic fields (EMF), a form of non-ionising radiation.

Unlike ionising radiation, such as X-rays, this type of radiation does not have enough energy to directly damage DNA.

Research published in 2024 led by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) looked at data from over 250,000 mobile phone users and found use of mobile phones was not associated with risk of developing brain tumours.

However, there are some concerns about whether prolonged exposure could have other biological effects.

Some research has suggested possible links between mobile phone use and changes in testosterone levels, sperm motility and cardiac activity.

These findings have fuelled concerns, particularly around carrying phones close to the reproductive organs or heart.

But the evidence is far from conclusive.

Most studies examining electromagnetic radiation and its effects on human organs, including the heart, have found little evidence of a direct relationship.

However, one major UK longitudinal study found an association between longer weekly mobile phone use and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

The research found that sleep patterns, psychological distress and neuroticism accounted for between 2.25 and 11.5 per cent of the association.

Importantly, researchers suggested that the way people use their phones could be part of the problem.

READ MORE Facing fossil fuel criticism, Albanese urges world not to overlook Pacific climate plight

Late-night scrolling, disrupted sleep, constant notifications and the psychological stress of an endless stream of digital information can all affect the body's circadian rhythms, hormone regulation and metabolic health.

Poor sleep and chronic stress are already well-established risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

The researchers noted that these factors could help explain the relationship, although the study could not establish causation.

title: US resumes flights after air traffic problem sparks chaos

The United States has lifted its order to ground all flights across the country after earlier communications problems at regional air traffic control centres.

title: 20,000 complaints a minute. How was the Microsoft outage fixed?
text:
Key Points Microsoft said services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications after the outage.

The disruption could result in over half a billion dollars in insurance claims, as billions more likely lost in productivity.

The Microsoft outage, which crippled popular services like Outlook and Teams, cost users over half a billion dollars, according to one expert.

Friday's outage lasted over 24 hours and prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars, and hosting virtual meetings.

Microsoft had over 450 million paid user licenses as of January 2026, according to its financial reporting, and over one billion devices connected to its services.

Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS told Reuters.

De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between US$300 million ($443 million) and US$500 million ($738 million).

Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.

Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.

READ MORE Microsoft says sorry for 24 hours-long global outage

Experts say the latest outage is a wake-up call for companies and users to have a backup plan for when services go offline.

How to prepare for future outages

RMIT Associate Professor of engineering Mark Gregory said companies in Australia have already been advised to plan for national telephone network outages after a series of failures.

"So if you're a Telstra customer, you need to have an Optus SIM card or something on another network as a backup," he told SBS News.

"If you're an Outlook or Microsoft user, you keep a Google or Gmail account as a backup so that you're still able to communicate or receive emails," Gregory said.

It's also important for companies, businesses, individuals and families to also have backups of software systems so that alternatives are available when one system fails, he adds.

He said businesses should also consider backups for human resource programs, billing, invoicing and accounting software.

"Unfortunately, I see many businesses that are not prepared to look at having that redundancy or backup approaches, and they simply rely upon everything being available," he said.

"And when it's not, their staff are really just being left in limbo."

Gregory said Australian businesses should have a mechanism to claim compensation, and the government should be able to fine big tech for outages that impact productivity.

"The loss of productivity will be in the tens of millions in Australia and tens of billions globally," he added.

What was the problem and how was it fixed?

Microsoft said the outage — one of the longest in Microsoft's history — was caused by server issues. The incident hit features tied to Exchange Online — mainly its cloud-based email and scheduling hub.

The company said a core process on the affected servers had become "overwhelmed". Once that happened, automated health checks within the system started shutting them down, tech expert Val Quinn told 7News on Saturday.

While the solution to the outage was to turn on the servers again, it wasn't that simple, Quinn added.

By the time the Microsoft engineers were ready to flip the switch on again, there was a huge reservoir of emails and messages queued up. Loading them all on in one go could create more problems, so they had to carry out the switch-on in stages, Quinn said.

Doug Jacobson, Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Iowa State University, said in a report on The Conversation that the pent-up messages were akin to a major highway crash.

Once the staged switch-on happens, email traffic does not instantly return to normal speed. Processing those long queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time — typically hours to days.

Is the crisis over?

Microsoft said that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications, ending the global outage that crippled online communications across businesses and governments for over 24 hours.

Dr Mohammad Goudarzi, from Monash University's Faculty of Information Technology, said engineers had been working to contain the outage's impact and restore services.

"Normally, in large-scale and interconnected systems, like Microsoft cloud platforms in this case, detecting a disruption may be quick, but identifying its underlying cause can take considerably longer," he told SBS News.

"These disruptions can also continue after access returns. Organisations may need to clear backlogs, check unfinished work and catch up on delayed decisions. Restoring the technology is only one part of restoring normal operations."

With additional reporting from Reuters

title: Dutch government collapse staved off, but crisis over tax policy continues
text:

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten has staved off the imminent collapse of his minority government after marathon talks on Saturday.

The government however remained embroiled in a political crisis over tax policy.

Following more than seven hours of crisis talks with his coalition partners, during which the government's future hung by a thread, Jetten emerged to reveal they would stay together, for now.

"In recent days, many good things have happened, but also things that have not gone well... we have to do better," Jetten said.

"This coalition is effectively dead. We just have to wait for the funeral to take place," Wilders said.

Wilders had sparked elections in 2025 when he pulled his party out of government in a row over immigration.

Against the odds, Jetten pulled off a stunning election win last year, coming from behind to defeat Wilders by a wafer-thin number of votes.

Jetten won widespread praise for his campaign, pushing a positive message and showing that the far right could be defeated in Europe.

After four months of haggling with the CDA and VVD leaders to form a coalition, he was finally sworn in as prime minister in February, becoming the country's first openly gay leader.

title: The Microsoft outage is part of a growing trend. This is how to prepare for further disruption
text:
Today's Microsoft outage has highlighted the risks of relying on cloud-based communications and Australians should be expecting more disruptions in the future, one expert says.

RMIT Associate Professor of engineering Mark Gregory says companies are not applying best practice in their processes.

"If we look at the outages that have occurred with Optus and Telstra, and also Vodafone, in some way they've all related back to a reduction in the amount of funds being put into the engineering side of the business," he said.

"So that when equipment goes down, or it's misconfigured, you then end up with a catastrophic outcome."

A major Telstra mobile outage in July that sparked chaos, with Triple Zero calls and businesses affected, was linked to the failure to maintain ageing equipment.

Gregory said engineering processes developed over hundreds of years generally follow a path of testing, checking with small groups, small pilot platforms and testing again before changes are rolled out.

"But that process is often either not used, or it's shortened because of the timelines that companies place on their engineering teams."

The Microsoft outage on Friday disrupted the use of popular programs such as Outlook and impacted the Australian Federal Police and Australian Security Intelligence Organisation.

Microsoft reported a widespread outage on Friday that left users unable to access Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft services. Source: Getty / Scott Olson

Gregory said a network misconfiguration — when settings don't match what the network expects — appears to have resulted in some cloud servers being disconnected from Outlook.

"Unbelieveably, they've had to reboot them to get them to rejoin the cloud," Gregory said.

He said businesses are trying to speed up the process of making changes, updates or improvements to their software and systems, and this is coming at a cost.

"The updates have been coming very quickly nowadays compared with what we experienced 10 or 15 years ago."

These frequent updates, along with increasing hacking attacks, have seen a rise in outages in recent years, but there are actions businesses and individuals can take to minimise the disruption.

What can Australians do?

Gregory said companies in Australia have already been advised to plan for national outages of telephone networks after a series of failures.

"So if you're a Telstra customer, you need to have an Optus SIM card or something on another network as a backup."

It's also important for companies, businesses, individuals and families to also have backups of software systems so that alternatives are available when one system fails.

"If you're an Outlook or Microsoft user, you keep a Google or Gmail account as a backup so that you're still able to communicate or receive emails," Gregory said.

Software is increasingly connected to cloud servers and he said businesses should also consider backups for human resource progams, billing, invoicing and accounting software.

"Unfortunately, I see many businesses that are not prepared to look at having that redundancy or backup approaches, and they simply rely upon everything being available," he said.

"And when it's not, their staff are really just being left in limbo.

The worst possible outcome is where companies order staff to take leave, which some of them do.

"Therefore, the problem becomes one that the staff have to carry."

In the past, businesses stored data and software programs within their own systems and offices.

"Due to the cost of doing that, over time companies have migrated their email into the cloud to use Office 365 or other hosted solutions," he said.

But Gregory said businesses are starting to understand the importance of having greater control over their services.

Businesses are increasing relying on cloud services rather than storing data and systems on their own in-house servers. Source: Getty / Jetta Productions Inc

"If you have your systems and services being provided from a long way away, such as the United States or Asia, the chances of failure increase," he said.

"'[Locating] them locally — such as within their own business or within the cloud situated in Sydney or Melbourne or Brisbane — you do see less outages when that occurs."

The advantage of this approach could be seen during the Microsoft outage as businesses whose emails were hosted by a company separate to the Microsoft Exchange Online, were still able to use programs such as Outlook despite the wider disruption.

'Part of our daily lives'

SBS has previously spoken to experts who say it's time for individuals and businesses to stop putting so much data and other information online, but Gregory said the computerisation of business processes is probably not going to change.

"It's a typical part of our daily lives today," he said.

"The question for many organisations has to be whether they rely solely upon cloud solution providers, or do they utilise alternative approaches such as self-hosted [services] or having those software packages run within the organisation."

Gregory said organisations need to work out the best options for themselves so they can still operate when these incidents occur.

"The only downside of course is cost," he said.

"You're paying for this alternative solution. [But] it's very difficult for companies to have hundreds or thousands of staff sitting around looking at computers unable to do anything, it's not productive.

Gregory says organisations also need address hacking attacks, which are on the rise partly because AI is making them easier.

"Nearly every major organisation in Australia has been hacked," he said.

"Quite often it's been because of a reluctance by the management teams and those organisations to actually spend the money that's needed to protect the company from hackers."

He believes the fines for failing to adopt best practice approaches are very low, and so companies were still underspending.

"The next phase will be class actions and people suing companies for losing their personal data," he said.

"And we really need to see more of that because Australia is still being hacked too often."

title: Cricket's war of words ramps up as Warner claims Khawaja was thrown 'under the bus'
text:
In brief Sandpapergate reemerged this week after Usman Khawaja claimed the entire team knew about the 2018 ball-tampering plot.

Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins denied the allegations, prompting a rebuke from David Warner.

Former cricketer David Warner has accused Pat Cummins of throwing Usman Khawaja "under the bus" after the Australian cricket captain rejected claims that the whole team was aware of the 2018 ball-tampering plot.

During a 70-minute press conference on Friday morning, Cummins broke his silence about sandpapergate, saying Khawaja's version of events was "complete and utter nonsense".

The scandal resurfaced this week after Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, claimed in his new autobiography, Sabr, that the entire team knew about ball tampering during the third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.

The allegations contradict the findings of a Cricket Australia investigation, which found Cameron Bancroft, who was filmed placing sandpaper down his cricket pants on the field, Steve Smith and Warner were the only ones involved in the ball-tampering, and it was a one-off incident.

The trio were subsequently suspended and fined.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Warner, who earlier this week said Khawaja's claims were "100 per cent accurate", on Friday defended Khawaja and hit back at Cummins.

"I still stick by Uzzie and what he's written in that book, because it is the truth, and I really, really support him," Warner said on Fox Cricket.

"I actually feel for him at the moment. I actually feel that today, the captain threw Uzzie under the bus, and I’m very, very disappointed about that.

"All three of us [Warner, Bancroft, Smith] have paid a big price in this thing. I hadn’t spoken about it in eight years, but at the end of the day, we’ve got to live with these consequences daily. We've been served a life punishment."

Warner stood by his claim that the Cricket Australia investigation had been mismanaged.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence. I feel like it was a botched investigation," he said.

"It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us, and we had to move on and just accept responsibility, the three of us, and we ultimately did.

"We don't have that opportunity to go there and speak again. [Cricket Australia CEO] Todd Greenberg squashed that the other day. There probably are going to be conversations behind the scenes after this."

Warner later added he would one day tell his side of the story and he was "not going to accept until the truth is out there".

Cricket Australia has stood by its findings, with Greenberg saying on Tuesday it would not reopen the investigation.

Khawaja has faced criticism over the timing of his allegations, which coincide with the release of his book.

Cummins: 'Complete and utter nonsense'

Earlier on Friday, Cummins rejected Khawja's claims, saying: "When [Usman Khawaja] says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong."

"I have said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening, but I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that."

He also alleged there had been ball tampering during an earlier match.

Cummins said those claims were "complete and utter nonsense".

Cummins said Khawaja was a friend but "friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations".

"In his book, Uzzie's been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell his story 100 per cent," he said.

"I'm really glad that he feels like he can. But we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Khawaja said in his book that he told Bancroft to be careful and avoid being scapegoated when the scandal unfolded.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper," he said.

"That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman ... that has been part of a team that's helped rebuild this Australian cricket culture over the last eight years."

Cummins said the culture of the 2018 side was very different to the current team.

"At that stage I think [the side] had a win-at-all-costs mentality, had an ugly underbelly, and there were too many silos within the team," he said.

"Traits that I hope that everyone's seen, and I try very hard to eradicate for the last six years as captain."

Some claims 'probably defamatory'

Cummins said he had received advice some of the claims were "probably defamatory" but he would not be taking any legal action.

"You got to move on. It's been eight years," he said.

"You got to draw a line at some point."

Cummins said parts of Khawaja's allegations were likely true but other parts were "vague".

"Some of these things are probably true, and they are his accounts of what happened. But I think there's a few big leaps here where he's being vague and I think the details really matter in that difference," he said.

"Perhaps there was conversations with Cameron Bancroft around taking sandpaper out and how to do it. That doesn't mean that everyone in that dressing room knew what was going on.

"The way he's presented his story, I think he's done it in a very casual manner, and it affects a lot of people. That's what I'm grappling with at the moment because I don't think it's okay."

Cummins saw ball-tampering in Sheffield Shield match

Cummins said the only other time he saw illegal ball-tampering was during a Sheffield Shield match, when a senior batter, who he chose not to name, brought a bottle cap onto the pitch.

"It was dealt with. The umpires knew it as well. They caught him out and said, 'You've got to stop that right now.' It was dealt with. That's the only time I had seen something illegal out there," he said.

Cummins has also addressed footage published by The Australian newspaper on Thursday of what appeared to be a heated argument with his wife.

"We weren't having a spat. Becky was very frustrated, animated, and really not happy with Usman," he said.

"It's half very comical. Becky wears her heart on her sleeve. And half all a bit ridiculous, isn't it? We are here talking about something that was dealt with eight-and-a-half years ago.

"Now I'm walking my one-and-a-half-year-old daughter with nappies out the front and I got cameras chasing me and my family. For me, that's a bit ridiculous."

Others from the 2018 side have also issued denials.

Australian fast bowler Mitchell Starc, who in 2021 stated he had no knowledge of the ball-tampering, said on Tuesday his recollection had not changed.

Mitch Marsh, who was part of the 2018 side, refused to answer questions on Wednesday about the allegations.

"There has obviously been a lot of noise around this week and I respect that certain people have told their stories, but I’m not here to share mine today."

title: Microsoft services not 'fully returned to baseline' as recovery from outage continues
text:
In Brief Microsoft said it is working to resolve an outage impacting "users in any region".

Popular business platforms Outlook and Teams have been impacted.

Schools, businesses, courts, and government agencies are still being affected by a global Microsoft outage, as the tech giant says it is working to restore services.

The company said it is "seeing early stabilisation and capacity improvements" as recovery efforts continue.

"Recovery actions are ongoing and have progressed in phases across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure.

"Global telemetry and customer reports show incremental improvement in several workloads; however, service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline," Microsoft said at 9pm (AEDT) on Friday.

Earlier on Friday, the company had expressed optimism, saying it was "seeing positive results" in restarting impacted systems, but shortly afterwards removed that detail from its updates.

Microsoft said it has "no evidence of malicious activity" associated with the incident.

'A chain reaction'

Governments in the Australian Capital Territory, Tasmania and Western Australia said they were impacted by the outage. Service NSW said some transactions were unavailable and encouraged customers to delay their visit or complete transactions online where possible.

Courts in South Australia and Victoria acknowledged the outage impacted court operations.

The Northern Territory Department of Education said schools across the state experienced technical issues. Tertiary educational institutions were also impacted, with Charles Sturt University and Macquarie University telling staff and students it was also impacting multi-factor authentication.

Federal authorities were caught up in the scramble, with the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) confirming they were both impacted by the outage.

Microsoft Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, OneDrive, Copilot, SharePoint Online, Defender XDR, Fabric, Graph, Intune, Planner, Purview, To Do, Power BI, Microsoft 365 Apps, Admin Center and Universal Print have all been impacted by the outage, according to Microsoft's Service Health Status site.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told reporters on Friday morning that he had spoken with Lieutenant General Michelle McGuinness, the National Cyber Security Coordinator, and Jane Livesey, president of Microsoft Australia and New Zealand.

He said Microsoft believed it was dealing with "an update that has gone awry" similar to the CrowdStrike outage in July 2024.

"One thing we had with CrowdStrike was we also have a whole lot of downstream impacts where it was affecting the capability of a whole range of other products quite separate from that," Burke said.

Alex Potanin, associate professor in computer science at the Australian National University, said outages like this have significant flow-on effects.

"It's usually a chain reaction," he said.

"It wasn't just Outlook. It was also Teams and other parts of their overall server infrastructure."

While cloud systems can bring businesses more convenience and lower costs compared to hosting locally, a key provider suffering an outage can flow through to other interconnected systems.

How did the outage happen?

In the early hours of this morning, Microsoft first acknowledged it was investigating issues relating to Teams functionality for users in North America.

The next update from the company expanded the issue to "users in any region", noting reports of difficulties accessing email inboxes through their Outlook and Microsoft Exchange products.

The company said its infrastructure has been strained by "a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable".

"Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss," it said.

So far, it has been attributed to an issue with the servers completing a health check.

READ MORE Why we're still living with password rules their creator regrets

Potanin said this is a normal check that servers run to monitor their status.

"For example, am I being able to connect to the other servers? Am I being able to use my memory without making mistakes? Am I actually still part of the network?"

When a server detects an issue, it will go offline and not contribute to overall system processing until it is fixed.

With some servers shutting down, Potanin said "many of the servers that they use started picking up a lot more slack and getting overloaded".

"But it may take them a few more hours before they come back online, as far as we can tell from the reports that they're posting."

Microsoft is sending updates through its status page and X account.

How have Australian businesses been affected?

The financial impact has already been massive, as the systems have been down since 5am AEDT, a privacy and security expert said.

The cost to Australia would be billions of dollars, said Ashwin Pal, of risk advisory firm RSM Australia.

"That's not just direct, but indirect costs as well," he said.

"But a protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel's back for smaller entities."

He said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn't have a fallback.

"They're just at a standstill — if you don't actually have a plan B, then you've got a problem."

title: 'Even a snail would agree': Greta Thunberg takes aim at Australia
text:
In Brief Greta Thunberg addressed a crowd at the UN climate summit in Türkiye on Thursday.

After not appearing at previous COP events, the activist said she returned to call for urgent action.

Environmental activist Greta Thunberg has slammed Australia's track record on climate action at COP31 talks in Türkiye, saying "even a snail would agree" that the country needs to move faster.

The 23-year-old's appearance alongside speakers from Australia, Nepal, Rwanda and Gaza caused traffic chaos inside the United Nations' climate summit in Antalya on Thursday, which also heard criticism of Australia's ongoing mining approvals.

Australia's Energy Minister Chris Bowen will lead negotiations at the annual event, which has drawn more than 92,000 attendees, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrived on Wednesday for the leaders' summit portion of the event.

Asked whether she agreed with comments about Australia's slow record on climate action, Thunberg said her opinion was obvious.

"Even a snail would agree with that," she told the crowd.

A four-bedroom home in Montmorency, in Melbourne’s north-east, on a stepped triangular block sold for $1,475,000 at auction on Saturday, with three bidders pushing it over $200,000 above its reserve. One of a street of homes built by the same builder in the late 1970s, and backing onto a flora and fauna reserve, 30 McCarthy Grove sits on 928 square metres of lush green land, with a red-brick undercover terrace, polished floorboards, a ground-level rumpus room, an upstairs entertaining area and a secure double garage. The property was one of 773 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 57 per cent from 515 reported results throughout the week, while 89 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The preliminary clearance rate sits just below the 59 per cent from the previous week. There were almost 150 more auctions scheduled this week as the unusually quiet spring auction season ramps up in its final month before the Christmas and January break.

The Montmorency home had a listed reserve of $1.24 million, which Ray White Eltham agent and auctioneer Jackson Ball said was advertised “a little bit earlier” than the seven days before auction required by law. The earlier notice gave the vendors two weeks “to get a bit of a sense on what the reception would be from the market”, Ball said. The second storey of the house has views of the bush surrounding the property. Ray White Eltham The auction opened with a genuine bid of $1.1 million, jumped in $20,000 and $10,000 increments from three bidders, quickly passed the $1.24 million reserve – at which it was declared on the market – and hit $1.32 million. From there, two local families looking to upsize duked it out until the finish. The winning bidders were a couple with two children who attend nearby Montmorency South Primary School. It is difficult for young NRL players of Pasifika or New Zealand heritage who are expected to carry a torch for the family but at the same time hold ambitions to step away from their shadow. Changed eligibility rules have thrown up multiple challenges, including threats to the future of the Kangaroos, who play the Kiwis in the World Cup final on Sunday. Passion: Tonga’s Robert Toia. Getty Images Consider the case of 22-year-old Roosters premiership player Robert Toia, who represented Queensland and Tonga this year. Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters received a long text from the young centre late on the day before the NRL grand final, in which Toia declared his World Cup allegiance to Tonga – reneging on an earlier undertaking to Walters to represent Australia if selected. Walters was disappointed with Toia’s decision, particularly because it followed the defection days earlier of Titans and Maroons winger Jojo Fifita to Tonga in the World Cup. However, he understood that Toia, with a grand final to play the following day, wanted to clear his mind of the competing loyalties and the family pressure.

Advertisement

“I don’t hold any grudges,” says Walters. “They need to go where their heart is. I said that to both of them. There is a lot of pressure from their Polynesian families. But that’s OK. They are just doing what is best for them.” The passion of many NRL players, like Melbourne’s Eli Katoa, for their ancestral homelands, such as Tonga and Samoa, is almost endemic, while others face relentless pressure from their extended family to represent the land of their fathers – despite the pay disparity of $850 per game compared with the Kangaroos receiving $40,000 for the tournament. Loading New International Rugby League board eligibility rules will allow more players like Toia to elect to play for countries other than Australia. Under the rules in place for this year’s World Cup, players are eligible to be selected by the country where one of their grandparents was born. But the IRLB this week extended the criteria to cover the birthplaces of eight great-grandparents, meaning the supply of NRL players to Pacific countries competing in future World Cups will cover the next generation of players. Casey McLean, a 20-year-old centre, was born in Blacktown, plays for Penrith, represented NSW in Origin this year and will play for New Zealand in Sunday’s World Cup final. As the number of homegrown players of Pasifika and New Zealand heritage approximates half the NRL population, the eligibility rules both ensure the best players are available for the code’s big money earner, State of Origin, while also making international rugby league more competitive and therefore more lucrative in terms of TV rights.

Advertisement

The rules, however, run the risk of redistributing NRL talent among the World Cup countries, rather than growing it at both grassroots level in the emerging countries and in Australia itself. As players in the NRL increasingly commit to New Zealand, Tonga, Samoa, Fiji and England, the numbers in the pool available for the Kangaroos diminishes. The NRL threatens to become the English Premier League, whose riches attract the world’s best soccer players, reducing the availability of positions for players of English background. Significantly, England has not won a FIFA World Cup since 1966. Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters is concerned the number of Australian eligible players will decline. Getty Images Walters recognises the development problem ahead. “We need to have more avenues for players eligible only for Australia,” he says. “We need Australia to develop big forwards and probably wingers as well. The Polynesian players develop a bit quicker than the guys of Australian heritage only.” Pointing to the size difference at junior levels, he adds: “We also need to ensure Australian kids stay in the game.”

Advertisement

Walters concedes this year’s World Cup exposed the Kangaroos’ lack of depth in middle forwards. Australia’s starting props against Samoa in the World Cup semi-final were Tino Fa’asuamaleaui, who represented Samoa at the 2019 tournament, and Keaon Koloamatangi, who played for Tonga at the 2022 iteration. Both switched their allegiance to Australia and were desperately needed in the early clashes against Samoa. As it transpired, with Patrick Carrigan coming off the bench and running 163 metres, Australia won the battle up front. “We won the middle metres,” says Walters. “It was a real focus for us and will be in the final against New Zealand, with their big pack.” Related Article Exclusive

Rugby League World Cup ‘All I want to do is put the red jersey on’: Eli Katoa’s road to recovery The IRLB has not yet resolved whether to categorise Tonga and Samoa as Tier 1 countries, which would require players to commit to them permanently. A 12-month grace period is being considered, allowing players to finally declare their permanent allegiance. It also allows the board time to consider whether there are any unintended consequences of the changed eligibility rules. Toia was born in Auckland but moved with his large family to Brisbane at age six. Toia agonised over his decision to play for Tonga before informing Walters. He may now be required to choose again.

Advertisement

The IRLB must question whether they are exerting too much stress on young players who are already besieged by pressure from their extended families. Some may choose not to play at all. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday. Sign up for our Sport newsletter.

From Treasuries to turbocharged tech bets, almost nothing on Wall Street is escaping the whiplash. Investors keep pouring billions into the fray anyway. Another rout in chipmakers dragged stocks lower on Friday (US time), even as inflation data eased fears of more aggressive Federal Reserve rate increases. It was the latest twist in weeks of violent reversals, with oil prices surging before dipping, bond yields lurching and the sudden downfall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang shaking one of the bull market’s biggest bets. Inflation fears keep upending bets on the US Federal Reserve tensions with Iran won’t stop jolting oil prices, and confidence in the AI boom remains shaky. Peter Morgan Beneath the relative resilience of major stock benchmarks, the difference between a windfall and a painful loss has often come down to market timing. The S&P 500 has moved an average of 1.6 per cent a day so far in November and the Nasdaq 100 an even more bruising 2.4 per cent, the largest average daily moves for both since the tariff turmoil of April 2025. Bonds have offered little refuge. The two-year Treasury yield had climbed nearly 28 basis points this month before Friday’s retreat, following similarly large moves in opposite directions over the previous two months. A popular long-term Treasury ETF has endured its own reversals, while volatility in an iShares fund tracking the classic 60/40 stock-and-bond portfolio has jumped. Professional trend-followers have been wrong-footed, suffering their biggest drawdown of the year.

Advertisement

Driving the tumult: inflation fears keep upending bets on the Fed, tensions with Iran won’t stop jolting oil prices, and confidence in the AI boom remains shaky. Related Article Aviation Inside Boeing’s mission to rebuild trust in the 737 after years of turbulence For Chris Davis, chairman of Davis Advisors, the unsettling part is how readily investors seem to be shrugging it all off. “The uncertainty is enormous, the fragility, the things that can go wrong very suddenly, enormous – combined with a tremendous amount of complacency in the market,” he said. Investors are embracing two distinct playbooks: buying the whole market through tried-and-tested index funds, or doubling down on the kind of speculative wagers that have delivered both spectacular gains and crushing losses this year. Vanguard’s flagship S&P 500 fund attracted nearly $US24 billion ($35.5 billion) in October, while a triple-leveraged semiconductor ETF pulled in $US9 billion despite losing half its value. Even as Nvidia’s upheaval rattles the artificial intelligence trade, demand for Anthropic’s planned blockbuster initial public offering has exceeded the shares available several times over.

Advertisement

The S&P 500, with a 2.5 per cent rally, staged its first weekly advance since early October, even as just a small group of its members is trading at their 52-week highs. The Nasdaq 100 added 3.5 per cent in the five-day stretch. For some professional investors, the message from the bond market is reason enough to stay cautious. Skyler Weinand, chief investment officer of the $US4.5 billion shop Regan Capital in Dallas, says 10-year Treasury yields could stay above 5 per cent for the foreseeable future, and the Federal Reserve will continue to increase interest rates. “We are staying in higher-quality, defensive names that aren’t taking on additional debt and are producing ample cash flows,” he said. “We are in the same camp of running minimal leverage and staying defensive until we see better downstream gains from AI.” Retail buyers have poured tens of billions of dollars into equity funds over the past two weeks. They’ve also been snapping up leveraged funds after sharp declines in assets at the start of November, raising the possibility that dip buying could help stabilise the battered technology trade. Among the more aggressive wagers, a group of double-leveraged Nvidia ETFs have attracted roughly $US900 million over the past week, even as the chipmaker’s shares lost 13 per cent following the departure of its longtime chief executive officer.

Advertisement

For Joseph Crow, a 35-year-old retail investor from Connecticut, the turmoil offered a chance for a quick payday. On Tuesday, he says he wagered $US3000 on call options expiring in three days on the triple-levered Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF (SOXL), betting on a fast rebound in chip stocks. The conviction paid off the next day — Crow says he sold for roughly $US23,000. Related Article Executive shake-up ‘I don’t care’: Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO “It was definitely a lotto purchase,” he said. “Seeing Nvidia so beaten down, it was like, ‘Man, something’s gotta lift eventually.’” For all the money chasing quick fortunes, the familiar index funds continue to exert a powerful pull. Vanguard’s VOO and VTI, iShares’ IVV, State Street’s SPY and SPYM and Invesco’s QQQ have captured about 30 per cent of all equity ETF flows this year, a share that’s been rising sharply since 2023, according to Athanasios Psarofagis at Bloomberg Intelligence. VOO alone has absorbed about $140 billion in 2026, a sum that puts it on pace for a record annual inflow. All told, the market’s violent swings have created booms and busts for those trying to ride them, while reinforcing the appeal of a simpler approach: owning the market rather than trying to pick winners and losers.

Washington, DC: Australia should be given priority access to the most capable artificial intelligence tools developed in the US and the Trump administration was wrong to temporarily withhold access to the powerful Claude Mythos tool. That’s the view of Lori Trahan, the Democratic congresswoman for Massachusetts, helping to lead a push for more stringent regulation of AI in the US. Lori Trahan, Democratic congresswoman for Massachusetts. Bloomberg She believes that as part of the push for better “rules of the road” to ensure the technology is properly controlled, the US should also foster more open collaboration with its Five Eyes intelligence partners, particularly Australia and the UK. “Innovation and safety are not at odds with each other, and I think we should just remind ourselves that when we set those standards high, we bring the rest of the world with us. But that’s also incumbent on our collaboration with our allies,” she said.

In April, Anthropic released its Claude Mythos AI model, which is particularly skillful at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in IT systems. Australian government security agencies and even Australian citizens working on AI in the US – along with all other foreign nationals – were initially barred from working with Mythos after a Trump administration edict, which was partly wound back after a couple of months. Claude Mythos was developed by Anthropic. Bloomberg Anthropic, which makes the Claude AI chatbot and is on the verge of a record $USD1.4 trillion initial public offer, has heavily restricted access to Mythos to financial institutions, major tech companies and cloud services providers like Amazon. Trahan, who is a member of Congress’ House Committee on Energy and Commerce, told this masthead the technology should not have been withheld from Five Eyes intelligence partners. “We rely on those relationships with our allies, and so I think that there’s a collaboration that we need to strike. In fact, we should have a Western stack [a collection of software tools] that is unified and fostering collaboration,” she said.

Advertisement

Anthropic says it wants to train its popular Claude models in Australia. Bloomberg Speaking at the Takeoff AI conference in Washington DC, Trahan said “there’s no question that AI was on the ballot” during the recent mid-term elections and that exit polls showed “that AI mattered in the congressional races”. There is a growing push in the United States for greater AI regulation and safeguards and Trahan, working alongside California Republican Jay Obernolte to achieve bipartisan reforms, has helped lead the way. The Australian government recently announced an AI Safety Institute in response to a push for greater regulation of artificial intelligence domestically, something which has been anathema to the Trump administration. Trahan thinks the position of the Trump administration could shift now the Democrats have a majority in Congress. “You never know what deal the president will sign,” she said.

title: Nvidia’s Huang is not alone. Here are some of the costliest affairs in history
text:

In the words of the normally sombre Economist magazine, it could go down as “the most expensive shag in history”. Following Nvidia boss Jensen Huang’s admission of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, some $US500 billion ($738 billion) has been wiped from the value of his AI firm. Speculation is also growing that his wife, Lori, may file for divorce following claims he had a second affair with a married employee. If she does so, she could be in line for a $75 billion payout – making her one of the world’s richest women and leaving Huang to rue some of the costliest infidelity ever. Yet a glance at history shows that he is not alone – as business leaders, politicians, sportsmen and kings have all learnt the hard way … Jeff Bezos and MacKenzie Scott divorced in 2019. Scott was left with a 4 per cent stake valued at about $US38 billion at the time of the divorce. AP Prime spot for price In terms of sheer, eye-watering expense, the costliest affair in history was conducted by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. Then the world’s richest man, Bezos began a secret romance with Lauren Sanchez, a married former Fox News presenter, in early 2018. It didn’t stay secret for long. The following year the National Enquirer published lurid details of his romance with Sanchez, including private text messages. Bezos and his wife, MacKenzie Scott, divorced six months later, with her receiving 4 per cent of Amazon stock, valued then at $56 billion. It remains one of the largest divorce settlements in history. Tiger Woods and then-fiancee Elin Nordegren. Detroit Free Press Woods in the rough In 2009, golfer Tiger Woods seemingly had the world at his feet – both on and off the course. With 14 major championships under his belt and a string of lucrative sponsorships, he had become the first sportsman ever to earn more than $US1 billon. Meanwhile, his marriage to his Swedish wife, Elin Nordegren, seemed the very picture of domestic bliss. Then, that November, reports emerged of an affair with a former New York nightclub hostess, Rachel Uchitel. Two days later, after a late-night confrontation with his wife, a shoeless, dishevelled Woods drove off at speed from his house, only to crash into a tree in a neighbour’s garden. Numerous other women came forward claiming infidelity with the golfer, whose subsequent divorce settlement was said to be worth hundreds of millions. The scandal also cost him vast amounts in cancelled sponsorship deals and affected his game. It was not until 2019 that he won another major trophy.

That footage of Andy Byron and Kristin Cabot at a Coldplay concert. TikTok Kiss-cam cost Few affairs have been exposed in such toe-curlingly embarrassing fashion as the one between US tech-firm boss Andy Byron and his employee Kristin Cabot. Last year the pair went to a Coldplay concert near Boston, enjoying complimentary VIP balcony seats. Unfortunately, a live feed of the concert on a big screen then panned to the happy couple just as they enjoyed a romantic clinch. “Either they’re having an affair or they’re just very shy,” remarked Coldplay’s Chris Martin as Cabot tried to cover her face while Byron ducked out of sight. Footage of the clip quickly went viral, and while the pair later denied that it was technically an affair – both were separating from their partners at the time – each quit the tech firm, Astronomer, shortly afterwards. As the company’s HR director at the time of the incident, Cabot should perhaps have known better than to mix business with pleasure. Yet as a result of “Coldplaygate” she received a stream of online abuse calling her a “home-wrecker” and later complained of being rendered unemployable. “I became a meme, I was the most maligned HR manager in HR history,” she said. David Petraeus, then commander of the NATO International Security Assistance Force, with Paula Broadwell, his biographer, in Afghanistan in 2011. NYT Warrior Monk with a wandering eye During America’s 20-year War on Terror, General David Petraeus was the man the White House turned to at the (not infrequent) moments it all went pear-shaped. Venerated for his thoughtful hearts-and-minds policies, the “Warrior Monk” masterminded two successful “troop surges”, in Iraq and Afghanistan, and in 2011 was appointed director of the CIA. Then, just as he was being tipped as a future Republican presidential candidate, news broke of an extramarital affair between him and his biographer, Paula Broadwell. He promptly resigned, and in 2015 was also fined $US100,000 ($148,000) for passing Broadwell classified information. His rumoured presidential bid never happened. Instead, the 2016 Republican candidate was one Donald J. Trump. Gary Hart and Donna Rice in 1987. Getty Images

Advertisement

Too much monkey business In the 1980s, Colorado senator Gary Hart was considered one of the Democrats’ best prospects since John F. Kennedy. Charismatic, Yale-educated and handsome, he quickly emerged as the frontrunner for the party’s nomination for 1988’s presidential election. Yet despite being hailed as the leader of a new generation, he expected the United States’ media to observe old-school rules about not reporting politicians’ private indiscretions. Times, however, had changed, and in May that year the National Enquirer published pictures of Hart on a yacht with Donna Rice, a woman 20 years his junior, sitting on his lap. It didn’t help that Hart was wearing a T-shirt named after the vessel, which was called Monkey Business. He then withdrew from the presidential race, which was won by Republican George H. W. Bush. John Profumo leaves the War Office with his wife Valerie Hobson in 1963 as he prepared to make a statement at the House of Commons about his affair with Christine Keeler. PA Images via Getty Images Never had it so bad … What was arguably the most notorious fling in modern Britain began in 1961, when John Profumo, the Harrow-educated secretary of state for war in Harold Macmillan’s administration, met 19-year-old model Christine Keeler at a society party at Cliveden House, the seat of Viscount Astor. Profumo – a friend of Queen Elizabeth II – then embarked on an affair with Keeler, yet denied any impropriety in a statement in the House of Commons two years later. Christine Keeler in her London flat in 1963. Mirrorpix via Getty Images A police investigation then proved he had lied, while Keeler later claimed to have also been sleeping with Yevgeny Ivanov, a Soviet naval attache at Moscow’s London embassy. Profumo resigned in disgrace, living the rest of his life in near-anonymity as a charity worker in the East End. But the real damage done was to the ruling class that he embodied. The scandal not only torpedoed the credibility of the conservative government under Macmillan, it hastened the end of traditional “deference” towards “establishment” authority.

Peter and Catherine of Russia in 1756. Anna Rosina de Gasc, Getty Images Lover of the Russian queen Unhappy in her loveless, sexless arranged marriage to grand duke Peter of Russia, the future Catherine the Great embarked on a passionate affair with Stanisław Poniatowski – a tall, handsome Polish nobleman. With tongues wagging in the Moscow court, he was eventually banished, while Peter ascended the throne as emperor. The two lovers, however, stayed in touch, and when Catherine then became empress after her husband’s death, she helped install Poniatowski as king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania. Her support was more about geopolitics than a gesture of affection, however, and quickly backfired. Far from being a compliant Moscow pawn, Poniatowski then tried to shift his kingdom away from Russia’s influence, forcing Catherine to send in Russian troops. After a series of occupations and partitions, Poniatowski was forced to abdicate his throne in 1795, and the Polish-Lithuanian kingdom ceased to exist. The first meeting of Tudor king Henry VIII and his ill-fated wife Anne Boleyn, as imagined by painter Daniel Maclise in 1835. Getty Images A courtly affair In medieval times the British royal family did not generally have to worry much about media scandal: newspapers hadn’t been invented, and gossipy courtiers could quickly be hauled off to the Tower. Henry VIII, however, did have to suffer Pope Clement VII, in Rome, who refused to sanction his marriage to Anne Boleyn after his previous one to Catherine of Aragon failed to produce an heir. Facing excommunication, Henry secretly married Boleyn in 1533 anyway while still legally married to Aragon – an act of bigamy in Rome’s eyes. He then severed ties with the Catholic Church. It put Britain on the path to Protestantism, scientific advance and prosperity but also led to bloody internal conflict with Catholics and the English Civil War. Poor Boleyn was also later executed. If you happened to swim at one of Sydney’s ocean and harbour pools this past week, you couldn’t have missed the joyful Saltwater Sisters of Byron Bay.

Crowned in vibrant swimming caps and accompanied by laughter, chatter and salutations, the salty seven descended on 53 city swimming spots, from Lilli Pilli to Palm Beach, and Balmain to Bondi.

The Saltwater Sisters Helen Blair, Caitlyn Feldmann, Jenny Cruden , Rachel Sullivan, Kath Vaubell, Libby McQueen and Bec Prodger. Audrey Richardson

United via a Northern Rivers morning swim group, the women decided to swap their regular routines for a coastal adventure to celebrate friendship, community and finding your tribe later in life.

“It’s been wonderful,” says Jenny Cruden, the group’s most exuberant member. “We’re having a lot of fun. Our caps are a great talking point – everyone stops us to ask about what we’re doing, so we’ve been meeting all sorts of people.”

Chilly water temperatures early in the week didn’t put off the northern visitors, who proudly swim year-round, rain, hail or shine. “We always get out with a smile on our faces,” she says.

The women say they’ve formed strong connections through swimming over the past two to four years and these have deepened, with physical, mental and social benefits.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.
